title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
The journey for today





flowchart LR
  A[Question] --> B[Search]
  B --> C[Screen]
  C --> D[Appraise]
  D --> E[Extract]
  E --> F[Synthesise]
  F --> G[Write]






By the end of the lecture, you should be able to explain how every stage contributes to a review that is credible, transparent, and useful.

Welcome to Week 1. We will use this diagram as the organising spine for the whole lecture because a literature review is a connected sequence of decisions as well as a piece of writing. We will return to this sequence in every section and add practical detail as we progress. The quality of your final prose depends on the quality of your earlier decisions, since an unfocused question, a narrow search, or uncritical source selection will weaken even a beautifully written account. As we work through the lecture, keep one possible research topic in mind so that you can attach each concept to a subject that matters to you.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: A review is a map of knowledge
text:
A review is a map of knowledge
A useful literature review tells the reader:



Evidence state
Question answered




Established
What is supported consistently?


Contested
Where and why do studies disagree?


Uncertain
Which conclusions remain fragile?


Missing
What has not yet been examined adequately?



The review therefore maps both knowledge and uncertainty.

A map selects and organises features for a purpose rather than reproducing every physical detail of a landscape, and your literature review performs a similar function. You should represent the evidence fairly while giving the greatest attention to evidence that directly serves your research question. In the example on this slide, soil-carbon effects may be established under some management systems, contested across climates, uncertain over long timescales, and missing for a particular region. Uncertainty is a legitimate research finding, so you should represent it clearly rather than forcing the literature towards a firmer conclusion than the evidence supports.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Why researchers review literature

Prevent accidental duplication and identify valuable replication.
Locate a proposed study within existing knowledge.
Justify the research question, design, measurements, and analysis.
Identify established methods and recurring methodological weaknesses.
Demonstrate that conclusions arise from evidence rather than preference.







Important


A gap becomes persuasive when it is specific, supported, and researchable.




Duplication and replication describe different scholarly situations. Replication deliberately tests whether a result holds again, while accidental duplication repeats work without a clear reason. Previous studies can strengthen your research design by revealing useful instruments, realistic sample sizes, common confounders, analytical strategies, and ethical concerns. When you identify a gap, aim for a precise statement. “Short-term trials dominate the evidence, while multi-year UK field comparisons remain scarce” is more useful than “there is little research” because it identifies the existing evidence, the missing dimension, and the opportunity for a feasible study.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
From topic to contribution





flowchart LR
  T[Broad topic] --> K[Known evidence]
  K --> D[Disagreement]
  D --> L[Remaining limit]
  L --> Q[Focused question]
  Q --> C[Contribution]






Ask of every proposed project: What becomes clearer because this study exists?

Let us complete this first concept by following the sequence with reduced tillage as our broad topic. Existing evidence may show variable effects on yield, disagreement may relate to soil type and study duration, and a remaining limitation may be the absence of multi-year comparisons in a defined region. A focused question can then address that limitation. Your contribution can involve testing transferability, improving measurement, resolving inconsistent evidence, examining an underrepresented population, or synthesising fragmented findings. We will now examine how search behaviour affects our ability to discover this evidence landscape reliably.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
How searching commonly begins


Type a few familiar keywords.
Inspect the first page of results.
Download papers with promising titles.
Begin writing from the available PDFs.

This approach is useful for reconnaissance, yet it leaves ranking, vocabulary, coverage, and selection decisions largely uncontrolled.

This workflow is a natural starting point because rapid web searching produces results immediately. The order of those results is shaped by ranking systems that may use popularity, citations, recency, accessibility, and personalisation. We can therefore use an early search for reconnaissance, gathering vocabulary, authors, journals, and landmark studies before constructing a structured search. Consider whether another person could reproduce a method described only as “I looked on Google Scholar.” The difficulty shows why we need a transparent record of where, when, and how we searched.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
The hidden vocabulary problem
One idea may have many labels:
precision agriculture
OR precision farming
OR site-specific management
OR digital agriculture
OR smart farming
One label may also have several meanings. Search quality therefore depends on understanding the language of the field.

Researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and different academic disciplines may describe the same idea with different vocabulary. Your search can miss relevant evidence when an author uses an unexpected synonym, while a broad term such as resilience may retrieve psychological, engineering, ecological, and economic research. The first ten or twenty useful records can supply vocabulary for improving your query, which means that keywords are discovered as well as proposed. During reconnaissance, collect subject headings, abbreviations, older terminology, scientific names, spelling variants, and related phrases.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: Libraries and databases use structured records
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: Information literacy is a chain of judgements
text:
Information literacy is a chain of judgements





flowchart LR
  N[Recognise a need] --> F[Find evidence]
  F --> J[Judge credibility]
  J --> C[Connect findings]
  C --> U[Use responsibly]
  U --> R[Reference transparently]






Information literacy includes asking who created the evidence, why it was produced, how it was measured, and whether its claims are proportionate to its data.

Information literacy extends beyond operating a database because finding a source is only one link in the chain. You must recognise what you need, search appropriate places, judge each source, connect it with other evidence, use it ethically, and provide a traceable citation. For empirical work, you should also examine data provenance, measurement quality, missing observations, representativeness, and reproducibility. Professional presentation and peer review are useful signals, while your own inspection of methods and evidence remains essential. Effective searching begins with knowing precisely what information you require, so we will now focus the research question.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Broad topics produce broad searches



Dimension
Clarifying question




System and context
Which population, place, or environment?


Intervention or exposure
Which practice, condition, or change?


Comparison
What provides a meaningful contrast?


Outcome and time
Which result, measured over what period?




A broad topic is useful for initial orientation, and a formal search requires greater precision. We can narrow sustainable agriculture to UK winter wheat systems, reduced tillage, conventional ploughing as the comparison, grain yield and soil organic carbon as outcomes, and a minimum study period of three years. As you narrow your own topic, treat each boundary as an intellectual decision about relevance rather than merely a way of obtaining fewer search results.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: PICO and PECO organise the question
text:
PICO and PECO organise the question



Element
Meaning
Example




P
Population or system
UK winter wheat fields


I/E
Intervention or exposure
No-till management


C
Comparison
Conventional ploughing


O
Outcome
Yield and soil organic carbon



Question template: In P, how does I/E, compared with C, affect O within a defined setting and timeframe?

PICO is a thinking framework that helps you introduce useful specificity, and PECO may suit a question in which researchers observe an exposure instead of assigning an intervention. Some questions omit a comparison, while qualitative questions may use a different framework. As we assemble the example row by row, listen for remaining ambiguity. We still need to decide how no-till will be defined, which measure of soil carbon will be accepted, and what will count as a sufficiently long study.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Scope defines inclusion and exclusion





flowchart LR
  Q[Focused question] --> I[Directly relevant evidence]
  Q --> B[Useful background evidence]
  Q --> X[Out-of-scope evidence]






For a UK winter-wheat question:

a multi-year UK field trial may be directly relevant;
a European maize study may provide background;
a laboratory study of an unrelated crop may be out of scope.


Relevance exists on several levels. Direct evidence should carry the main argumentative burden in your review, while background evidence may explain mechanisms or wider context. You may find out-of-scope evidence interesting, although interest alone cannot justify inclusion. The scope decisions you make here will later become inclusion and exclusion criteria, reducing drift and protecting your review from selecting papers simply because their conclusions appear attractive.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: A good question is answerable and consequential
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: Build a concept map before writing syntax
text:
Build a concept map before writing syntax







Concept
Synonyms and variants




Winter wheat
“winter wheat”, wheat, cereal*


Reduced tillage
“no-till”, “zero tillage”, “reduced till*“,”conservation tillage”


Yield
yield, “grain yield”, productivity


Soil carbon
“soil organic carbon”, “soil carbon”, SOC



The concept map preserves the reasoning independently of any particular database.

A concept map is the portable version of your search strategy, so create it before worrying about database field codes. Each row represents a distinct idea from the research question, while the terms within a row represent acceptable ways of expressing that idea. A broader term such as cereal may improve coverage and may also introduce irrelevant records, so test its contribution. Include spelling variants, plural forms, abbreviations, scientific names, and controlled subject headings where the literature uses them.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Boolean logic connects the blocks
("winter wheat" OR wheat OR cereal*)
AND
("no-till" OR "zero tillage" OR "reduced till*" OR "conservation tillage")
AND
(yield OR "grain yield" OR productivity)

OR broadens within one concept.
AND requires different concepts to meet.
Parentheses preserve the intended grouping.


Read this string aloud as logic. A record may use any population term, must also use at least one tillage term, and must also use at least one yield term. Adding AND usually reduces the result set, while adding OR usually increases it. Parentheses work like brackets in arithmetic by controlling the order of interpretation. Use NOT cautiously because an exclusion can remove relevant records unexpectedly, and change one part of your search at a time so that you can explain why the result count changes.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Phrase searching, truncation, and proximity








Tool
Purpose
Example




Quotation marks
Keep words together
"soil organic carbon"


Truncation
Capture word endings
predict*


Wildcard
Replace character variants
database-specific


Proximity
Keep concepts near each other
artificial NEAR/3 intelligence



Symbols vary across platforms, so always check the database help page.

Let us consider each search tool carefully. Phrase searching prevents words from drifting apart. Truncation captures grammatical variants and can create noise when the stem is too short. Wildcards help with spelling variations, although their symbols differ between platforms. Proximity searching captures flexible phrasing that quotation marks would miss, such as soil appearing within three words of carbon. The underlying search logic transfers between databases, while the exact syntax must be adapted to each platform.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Test, inspect, and refine





flowchart LR
  D[Draft string] --> R[Run search]
  R --> I[Inspect 10-20 records]
  I --> V[Harvest vocabulary]
  V --> A[Adjust one block]
  A --> R






Stop refining when the search retrieves known relevant papers and produces an acceptable balance between coverage and noise.

Search development is iterative, much like experimental calibration. Inspect the titles, abstracts, and keywords of both promising and irrelevant records. Relevant papers reveal missing synonyms, while irrelevant papers reveal ambiguity that may require an additional concept or field restriction. A known-item check gives you a practical diagnostic: if your search cannot retrieve a clearly relevant landmark paper, investigate which part of the strategy prevented its discovery. Perfect precision and perfect recall are rarely achievable, so document and justify your stopping decision.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Live Scopus walkthrough


Open Scopus in a separate browser tab

We will now put the ideas from this section into practice in Scopus. As you watch the live page, follow how we move from the home search to the document search, choose appropriate fields, enter one concept block at a time, and compare the number and relevance of the retrieved records. We will inspect titles, abstracts, author keywords, and indexed terms so that you can see where additional vocabulary comes from. We will then combine the concept blocks, apply only defensible filters, save the exact query, and record the date and result count. If your browser or institutional access prevents the embedded page from loading, use the link beneath the frame to open Scopus directly; the same walkthrough sequence still applies.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: Use more than one suitable information source
text:
Use more than one suitable information source







Source type
Typical contribution




Multidisciplinary database
Broad journal and citation coverage


Subject database
Specialist vocabulary and disciplinary coverage


Citation searching
Earlier foundations and later developments


Repositories and grey literature
Theses, policy, technical, and organisational evidence



Different sources reveal different parts of the evidence landscape.

Your database choices should follow your question and discipline. Searching several poorly matched databases adds work without improving coverage, while complementary sources reduce blind spots. You can extend database searching through backward citation searching in reference lists and forward citation searching among papers that later cited a key study. Grey literature includes material produced outside conventional academic publishing, such as government reports and technical documents, and you should apply the same careful appraisal to these sources as you apply to journal literature.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: The search log is the memory of the review
text:
The search log is the memory of the review



Field
Example




Source
Scopus


Date
10 August 2026


Exact query
Saved without alteration


Fields
Title, abstract, keywords


Filters
2015-2026; articles; English


Results
286 records


Revision note
Added “conservation tillage”




Search results change over time because databases add records and interfaces evolve, which makes a precise date and exact query essential. Your log prevents repeated mistakes and allows a supervisor or collaborator to review the strategy. Screenshots can support the record, while saved query text remains easier to copy, inspect, and adapt. Save your queries in plain text and export database search histories where the platform provides that option.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: A mini-protocol fixes decisions before results
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Reproducibility strengthens credibility





flowchart TD
  T[Transparent search] --> S[Repeatable screening]
  S --> E[Consistent extraction]
  E --> A[Auditable synthesis]
  A --> C[Credible conclusions]






Reproducibility allows another person to understand, challenge, and improve the review.

Documentation strengthens scientific credibility. Because databases change, reproducibility does not guarantee that another person will obtain an identical set of records forever, yet your documentation should enable them to repeat your logic and understand your decisions. Transparency will also help you months later, when details would otherwise be forgotten. Your completed search creates a set of candidates, and we will now decide consistently which candidates belong in the review.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Search results are candidates





flowchart LR
  A[All records] --> D[Remove duplicates]
  D --> T[Title and abstract screen]
  T --> F[Full-text screen]
  F --> I[Included studies]






Every exclusion should follow a predefined criterion rather than an impression of whether the result is convenient.

The screening funnel narrows search results into the studies that address your question. Searches across several databases produce duplicate records, which you should remove before reporting screening counts. Title and abstract screening remains deliberately inclusive because unclear records should progress to full-text assessment. Full-text screening then applies your criteria with greater confidence. Aim for consistent relevance across decisions, remembering that a high-quality study may still be excluded when it answers a different question.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: Inclusion and exclusion criteria must be operational
text:
Inclusion and exclusion criteria must be operational







Vague criterion
Operational criterion




Recent studies
Published from 2015 to the final search date


Good evidence
Empirical study reporting design, sample, and outcome data


Relevant long-term studies
Wheat or barley field studies lasting at least three years



Operational criteria can be applied consistently by different reviewers.

Adjectives such as recent, relevant, robust, and long term require definitions before they can guide a reproducible decision. Imagine two reviewers applying each vague criterion on this slide and consider why they might reach different decisions. Your operational criteria should connect directly to the research question and planned synthesis. Apply them regardless of whether a study reports a convenient, inconvenient, statistically significant, or non-significant finding.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Read with a declared purpose
Before opening a paper, complete this sentence:

“We are reading this paper to determine whether …”

Then follow a rapid first-pass route:
Title → Abstract → Figures and tables → Headings → Conclusion → Methods
Promising papers then receive a complete, careful reading.

Purpose-led reading helps you avoid highlighting everything and remembering very little. Your purpose may involve checking a method, population, effect estimate, measurement approach, or explanation for disagreement. The first-pass route provides triage before complete reading. Figures and tables often reveal sample size, variability, and practical magnitude more clearly than the abstract. You should then inspect the methods before accepting the conclusion because the design determines which claims the evidence can support.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Separate claim, evidence, and warrant





flowchart LR
  E[Evidence] --> W[Reasoning or warrant]
  W --> C[Claim]






Ask:

What do the authors want us to believe?
Which observations and analyses support that belief?
Why should those results justify that conclusion?
Which alternative explanations remain possible?


The warrant is the reasoning that connects evidence to a claim. A study may report an association and then imply causation, creating a weak warrant even when the numerical analysis is correct. For example, farms adopting a practice may differ systematically from farms that do not, so an observed outcome difference may reflect selection as well as the practice itself. Paraphrase the claim and the evidence separately before judging whether the warrant connects them convincingly.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: Appraise the design, data, and analysis
text:
Appraise the design, data, and analysis



Domain
Questions




Design
Can the design answer the stated question?


Sampling
Who or what is represented?


Measurement
Are variables valid, reliable, and clearly defined?


Analysis
Do methods match the design and data?


Uncertainty
Are effect sizes, intervals, and limitations reported?


Transparency
Are methods, data, or code sufficiently documented?




Your detailed appraisal questions should match the study type. Randomised trials, observational studies, qualitative interviews, surveys, and modelling studies require different checks, although these broad domains remain useful across designs. Journal prestige and citation count provide contextual signals rather than direct measures of quality. Keep balanced notes by recording at least one specific strength and one specific limitation for each important study.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Credibility determines evidential weight
High relevance + strong methods      → central evidence
High relevance + serious limitations → cautious evidence
Lower relevance + strong methods     → contextual evidence
Lower relevance + weak methods       → limited influence
Critical appraisal guides how strongly a study influences the synthesis; it should never become a ritual checklist detached from interpretation.

Studies should contribute different amounts of weight to your argument. Counting how many papers support each conclusion treats every design and dataset as equal, which is rarely defensible. A small weak study should not cancel a large rigorous study simply because their conclusions differ, and one prestigious study should not silence a consistent body of evidence. Your synthesis should explain both quality and consistency. We will now organise these appraisal judgements across studies.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
section: Extract evidence into a common structure
text:
Extract evidence into a common structure



Field
What to capture




Citation
Author, year, venue


Context
Population, place, and timeframe


Design
Sampling, comparison, and sample size


Method
Measurements and analysis


Findings
Effect, direction, and uncertainty


Appraisal
Strengths, limitations, and bias risks


Relevance
Direct, contextual, or peripheral




A common extraction structure converts individual papers into comparable evidence. Copying abstracts provides too little methodological detail because abstracts emphasise headline findings. Use concise paraphrases and include page references for important details that you may need to verify. Your extraction table should contain enough information to support synthesis without becoming a second full copy of every paper.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Move from summaries to themes





flowchart LR
  P[Paper-level notes] --> G[Group by theme]
  G --> C[Compare findings]
  C --> X[Explain disagreement]
  X --> J[Judge confidence]
  J --> N[Identify next question]






Themes may be organised by method, population, intervention, outcome, mechanism, geography, or theoretical position.

An author-by-author sequence leaves the reader to discover relationships between papers, while thematic synthesis makes those relationships explicit. A thematic paragraph begins with a claim about the evidence, compares supporting and conflicting studies, explains methodological differences, and ends with a reasoned conclusion. Disagreement may arise from different populations, durations, measurements, analytical assumptions, or study quality. Explaining these differences gives your reader more insight than simply reporting that the results were mixed.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
Write comparative paragraphs
A useful paragraph sequence

State the thematic claim.
Present the strongest supporting evidence.
Introduce contrasting or qualifying evidence.
Explain likely reasons for the difference.
Judge the present level of confidence.
Connect the theme to the research question.


Let us model this sequence with a short example. Evidence that reduced tillage increases total soil carbon remains mixed; long-duration studies tend to report gains; shorter studies often report little change; and sampling depth and soil type explain part of the disagreement. Confidence is therefore stronger for surface carbon than total-profile carbon, while a long-term regional study could address the remaining uncertainty. This structure performs synthesis because it compares, explains, judges, and connects the evidence to a justified next question.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review
text:
The complete review remains auditable





flowchart LR
  Q[Question] --> S[Search log]
  S --> R[Screening record]
  R --> A[Appraisal notes]
  A --> E[Extraction table]
  E --> T[Thematic synthesis]
  T --> W[Written argument]









What is known with reasonable confidence?
What remains contested, and why?



What is still unknown?
Which next study is justified?



This final diagram reconnects every part of our lecture. Each arrow represents traceability, allowing your reader to see how the written argument arose from included studies and how those studies arose from explicit search and screening decisions. Apply the four final questions to the topic you have kept in mind throughout the session. The paired practical guide turns each lecture section into an activity that moves your own work from topic selection through to a synthesis plan. A credible review grows from transparent decisions, careful judgement, and a fair representation of uncertainty.
crumbs: Research Skills for a Credible Literature Review

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Question 1: Where is the centre?
This leads to measures of central tendency.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Question 2: How much do values vary around that centre?
text:
Question 2: How much do values vary around that centre?
This leads to measures of dispersion.
Together, these form the basic language of data description.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
1. It uses every observation
Every value contributes.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: 2. The deviations from the mean sum to zero
text:
2. The deviations from the mean sum to zero
\[
\sum (x_i - \bar{x}) = 0
\]
This means the mean perfectly balances positive and negative deviations.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: 3. It minimises the sum of squared distances
text:
3. It minimises the sum of squared distances
Among all possible choices of centre, the mean is the value that makes
\[
\sum (x_i - c)^2
\]
as small as possible.
This is one reason why the mean appears in regression and machine learning.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Case 1: odd number of observations
Order the values and take the middle one.
Example:
3, 5, 7, 10, 12
There are 5 observations, so the middle position is the 3rd.
Median = 7
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Case 2: even number of observations
Order the values and average the two middle values.
Example:
3, 5, 7, 10
The two middle values are 5 and 7.
Median = ((5+7)/2 = 6)

median(x)
median(c(3, 5, 7, 10))
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
1. It is resistant to outliers
Extreme values can move far away without changing the middle-ranked position much.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: 2. It works well for skewed distributions
text:
2. It works well for skewed distributions
Especially income, waiting times, and count data with long tails.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: 3. It is appropriate for ordinal data
text:
3. It is appropriate for ordinal data
If categories have an order but not equal intervals, the median may still make sense, while the mean may not.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
4. It minimises absolute deviations
The median is the value that minimises:
\[
\sum |x_i - c|
\]
This mirrors the mean’s role for squared deviations.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
The mean

uses all magnitudes
is mathematically elegant
is sensitive to outliers
minimises squared distance
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
The median

uses ordering, not full magnitude information
is robust to outliers
is ideal for skewed data
minimises absolute distance

Neither is “always better”.
They answer different questions.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: 1. It can be used for categorical data
text:
1. It can be used for categorical data
This is very important.
For categories such as:

favourite crop
transport mode
yes/no response
disease class

there may be no meaningful mean or median, but the mode still makes sense.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: 2. A dataset can have more than one mode
text:
2. A dataset can have more than one mode

one mode → unimodal
two modes → bimodal
more than two → multimodal
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: 3. It can be unstable in small samples
text:
3. It can be unstable in small samples
A small change in frequencies can change the mode.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
4. It may not be unique
If several values tie for highest frequency, there may be several modes.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Use the mean when:

values combine additively
outliers are not too influential
mathematical modelling requires it
interval/ratio interpretation is meaningful
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Use the median when:

data are skewed
outliers are strong
robustness matters
ordinal scale data are involved
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Use the mode when:

the question is about most common values or classes
the data are categorical
peaks in the distribution are substantively important
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Strength
It is quick and intuitive.
crumbs: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion

title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Weakness
It uses only two observations: the smallest and largest.
So it ignores almost everything in the dataset.
That means it is highly sensitive to outliers and unstable from sample to sample.

text:
Welcome: this is about data, not buttons
In this module, the goal is not “learning menus”.
The goal is learning how to think clearly about data:

What does one row mean?
What does one column mean?
What counts as “missing”?
How do we store repeated measurements?

We’ll use R because it makes data work:

transparent (you can see exactly what you did),
repeatable (you can re-run the same steps tomorrow),
transferable (the same ideas apply to any tool).

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
The 80–20 rule of data work
A common rule of thumb:

Most time goes into getting data into a usable shape.

What that includes:

designing a sensible table
cleaning and checking values
choosing consistent codes and units
reshaping (wide ↔︎ long)
combining files (joins) and summarising (aggregation)

If this part is done well, everything downstream becomes easier.

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
What is a dataset?
Think of a dataset as a table:

Rows = observations
Columns = variables
Cells = values

The most important question is:

What does one row represent?
(your unit of observation)

# Make rgl render as an htmlwidget in Quarto/HTML
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(rgl))
rgl::setupKnitr(autoprint = FALSE)

options(rgl.useNULL = TRUE)

# --- Dimensions (change these to match your story) ---
n_cols <- 6   # X
n_rows <- 5   # Y
n_time <- 10  # Z (make it longer than X/Y)

# Scale cube so Z is longer (like your diagram)

sy <- 1
sz <- 2  # <-- "time twice as long"

# IMPORTANT: rgl::cube3d() is a cube spanning [-1,1] in each axis.
# We want our cube to span [0,sx] × [0,sy] × [0,sz] to match the gridlines and axes below.
cube <- rgl::cube3d()
cube_s <- rgl::scale3d(cube, sx/2, sy/2, sz/2)

rgl::wire3d(cube_s, color = "#4e627f", lwd = 2)

gy <- seq(0, sy, length.out = n_rows)

# Lines parallel to Z at each (x,y)

Practical (10 min): make a messy table tidy

Code
# Here is a small demo data table using tibble's tribble function.
# What is a tibble? It's a modern version of a data frame, from the 'tibble' package, with cleaner printing and friendlier handling of column types.
# What is tribble()? It's short for "transposed tibble" and is a nice way to write out small tables by hand in code.
# The ~ (tilde) at the top sets the column names.
# Each line after gives the data for one row.

messy <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Plot,            # Column 1: Plot number (numeric)
  ~Fertiliser_raw,  # Column 2: Fertiliser name as raw messy text (character)
  ~Yield_and_Height,# Column 3: Yield and height in a single messy string (character)

  1, " fert a ", "7.2 t/ha; 85 cm",   # Row 1
  2, "FertB",    "5.8 t/ha; 78 cm",   # Row 2
  3, "A",        "7.0 t/ha; 82 cm"    # Row 3
)

# Print the resulting tibble
messy


Your goals:

create Fertiliser with consistent codes (FertA, FertB)
split Yield_and_Height into two numeric columns: Yield_t_ha, PlantHeight_cm

Hint (not the only way):


Code
# Step by step explanation:
library(dplyr)
tidy1 <- messy |>
  # 1. Clean up the Fertiliser_raw column.
# We want to remove extra spaces and ignore upper/lower case,
# so that different spellings of the same fertiliser are treated the same.

mutate(
  # Create a new column called Fertiliser
  Fertiliser = case_when(
    
    # If the cleaned text is "fert a" or just "a",
    # label it consistently as "FertA"
    str_to_lower(str_squish(Fertiliser_raw)) %in% c("fert a", "a") ~ "FertA",
    
    # If the cleaned text matches any of these versions of FertB,
    # label it as "FertB"
    str_to_lower(str_squish(Fertiliser_raw)) %in% c("fertb", "fert b", "fertiliser b") ~ "FertB",
    
    # If it does not match any of the known fertiliser names,
    # keep the original text unchanged
    TRUE ~ Fertiliser_raw
  )
) |>
  # 3. Split Yield_and_Height column (which looks like "7.2 t/ha; 85 cm") into two columns: Yield_raw and Height_raw (separated at the semicolon).
  separate(Yield_and_Height, into = c("Yield_raw", "Height_raw"), sep = ";") |>
  mutate(
    # 4. Pull out the numbers from Yield_raw and Height_raw. So "7.2 t/ha" becomes just 7.2, and "85 cm" becomes 85.
    Yield_t_ha = parse_number(Yield_raw),
    PlantHeight_cm = parse_number(Height_raw)
  ) |>
  # 5. Pick out just the columns we want, in a tidy order.
  select(Plot, Fertiliser, Yield_t_ha, PlantHeight_cm)

tidy1

section: Galton’s board: chance making a pattern
text:
Galton’s board: chance making a pattern
Drop many balls through pegs:

each bounce is random (left/right)
the sum of many small random steps produces a stable shape

This is a visual bridge to the Central Limit Theorem.

title: Data Foundations (R)

title: Data Foundations (R)
section: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): the idea
text:
The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): the idea
If you repeatedly take samples of size \(n\) and compute their mean:

the distribution of those means becomes approximately normal as \(n\) grows
even when the original data are not normal

What changes with \(n\):

the centre approaches the population mean \(\mu\)
the spread shrinks like \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
The CLT (clear statement)
Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) be independent draws from a distribution with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\) (both finite).
Define the sample mean: \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\)
Then, for large \(n\), \(\bar{X}\) is approximately: \(\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\)
Important: the CLT is about the mean of repeated samples, not about your raw data being bell-shaped.

title: Data Foundations (R)
section: CLT demo (R): start with a skewed distribution

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
Interpreting what you just saw
As \(n\) increases:

the distribution of \(\bar{X}\) becomes more symmetric (more bell-shaped)
it concentrates around the true mean ( \(\mu = 1\) here )
its spread shrinks (roughly proportional to \(1/\sqrt{n}\) )

This is one reason why averages are “stable” even when individual measurements are noisy.

title: Data Foundations (R)
section: Linking Galton’s board to the CLT
text:
Linking Galton’s board to the CLT
On Galton’s board:

each ball takes many small random left/right steps
the final position is the sum of those steps

Sums (and averages) of many small independent random influences tend to create:

a predictable centre
a predictable spread
and often a bell-shaped distribution

That’s the core intuition behind the CLT.

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
Section 3: Data types + measurement
In this section we separate two ideas:

how R stores a column (numeric / character / factor / ordered / Date)
what the values mean (continuous / interval / ordinal / categorical)

The second idea determines what summaries and comparisons make sense.

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
Data types in R (storage types)
R stores columns as types like:

numeric / integer: measurements, counts
character: text
factor: categorical values (levels)
ordered factor: ordinal categories with a known order
logical: TRUE / FALSE
Date / POSIXct: dates and date-times

Storage type is not the same as measurement scale, but they should agree.

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
Quick type check in R


Code
df |> glimpse()


What you’re looking for:

IDs stored as character (often!)
dates stored as Date, not character
numeric columns that are accidentally character because of messy entries

title: Data Foundations (R)
section: Measurement scale: what operations are meaningful?
text:
Measurement scale: what operations are meaningful?
Four common scale labels we’ll use:

Categorical (nominal): labels only (no order)
Ordinal: ordered categories (gaps not equal/known)
Interval: equal spacing, but zero is arbitrary (e.g., °C)
Continuous (ratio): equal spacing + meaningful zero (e.g., height, mass)

These determine what summaries are sensible.

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
Categorical (nominal)
Properties

categories/labels only
no inherent ordering

Good summaries

counts, proportions
bar charts

Examples

treatment group (Control, FertA, FertB)
species (oak, pine, birch)

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
Ordinal
Properties

categories have an order
distances between levels are not known to be equal

Good summaries

counts by level
median / percentiles (carefully)

Examples

Likert responses (Strongly disagree … Strongly agree)
disease severity (mild, moderate, severe)

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
Interval
Properties

differences are meaningful and equally spaced
zero is not “none” (it’s a reference point)

Good summaries

mean, SD; differences

Examples

temperature in °C or °F

title: Data Foundations (R)
text:
Continuous (ratio)
Why “ratio”?

They are called ratio variables because their scale has a true, meaningful zero — a value representing the complete absence of the measured quantity.
This means you can compare values by making ratios: 20 kg really is twice as much as 10 kg, and 0 kg truly means “none.”
Unlike intervals (where zero is arbitrary), on a ratio scale, both differences and proportions (ratios) make sense. This is why height, mass, and time are all “ratio” variables: you can say one object is twice as long, or half as heavy, as another.

Properties

equally spaced
meaningful zero (“none of the quantity”)
ratios make sense (20 kg is twice 10 kg)

Good summaries

mean/SD, median/IQR, histograms, scatterplots

Examples

height (cm), mass (kg), duration (seconds), distance (m)

Learning objectives
By the end of this session you should be able to:

Recognise and work with special values (NA, NaN, Inf, NULL)
Convert between data types safely
Work confidently with:

Vectors

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
What is a data object?

Everything in R is an object
Objects live in the Global Environment
Every object has:

A type (what it stores)
A class (how R treats it)


Example:
x <- 5
class(x)

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
Basic primitive types
a <- 1
mode(a)

a <- "1"
mode(a)

a <- TRUE
mode(a)

a <- 1i
mode(a)
Core primitive types:

numeric (double): real numbers with decimal values, used for most mathematical calculations
integer: whole numbers without decimals, often used for counting or indexing
character: text data, including letters, words, or symbols
logical: boolean values, either TRUE or FALSE
complex: numbers with real and imaginary parts, used in advanced mathematical computations

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
Checking type and class
x <- 5

class(x)
typeof(x)
mode(x)



Function
Purpose




class()
How R treats the object


typeof()
Internal storage type


mode()
Legacy type description

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
Special values
NULL

Absence of a value
Not even a vector

x <- NULL
is.null(x)

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
Behaviour of special values
When you perform arithmetic with NA, such as 5 + NA, the result is NA because the value is unknown and R cannot determine the outcome.
Calculating the mean of a vector that contains NA, like mean(c(1,2,NA)), returns NA because the missing value prevents the computation.
If you use the argument na.rm = TRUE, as in mean(c(1,2,NA), na.rm = TRUE), R removes the missing values before performing the calculation, and the result becomes 1.5.

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
Naming rules
Valid names:
x1 <- 5
5 -> x1   # reversing the arrow also assigns the value to x1
plant_height <- 10
yield_2024 <- 8
In R, the assignment arrow can point either left (<-) or right (->).
Both forms assign a value to a variable, but the left arrow is the standard and most commonly used style.
The right arrow is sometimes useful in pipelines or when you want to place the result at the end of a sequence of operations.
You can also use = for assignment:
x1 = 5
Use <- for most assignments in scripts and functions, as it is the conventional R style and avoids confusion with = used inside function arguments.
Use = mainly when specifying arguments inside functions, such as:
mean(x = c(1, 2, 3))
Avoid:

spaces
starting with numbers
special characters like @, #, %

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
Coercion
R will often convert types automatically.
c(1, 2, "3")
Result: character vector
Because R applies type coercion rules when combining different data types. In a vector, all elements must be of the same type, so R converts them to the most flexible type that can represent all values.
The coercion hierarchy is: logical → integer → numeric → complex → character.
Since character is the most flexible type, any mixture that includes a character value will be converted to character.

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
Checking and converting class
class() describes how R treats the object at a higher level
typeof() shows the internal storage type used by R
x <- "10"

class(x)      # "character"
typeof(x)     # "character"

For character data, class and typeof are the same because
there is no special higher-level structure applied.

x <- as.numeric(x)

class(x)      # "numeric"
typeof(x)     # "double"

For numeric data, class is “numeric” (a general category),
but typeof is “double” because R stores most numbers as double-precision floating-point values internally.

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
Creating an array
a <- array(1:24, dim = c(2,3,4))
This creates a three-dimensional array using the numbers from 1 to 24. The dim = c(2,3,4) argument tells R how to shape the data.
The dimensions mean:

2 rows
3 columns
4 layers (or “slices”)

So the array is structured as 4 separate 2×3 matrices stacked along a third dimension.
R fills arrays column-wise, just like matrices. That means it fills down the rows first, then moves across columns, and then moves to the next layer.
Layer 1 (a[ , ,1]):
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6
Layer 2 (a[ , ,2]):
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    7    9   11
[2,]    8   10   12
Layer 3 (a[ , ,3]):
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]   13   15   17
[2,]   14   16   18
Layer 4 (a[ , ,4]):
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]   19   21   23
[2,]   20   22   24
Indexing follows the order:
a[row, column, layer]
Examples:
a[1,1,1]  # first row, first column, first layer → 1
a[2,3,1]  # second row, third column, first layer → 6
a[1,2,3]  # first row, second column, third layer → 15
a[2,1,4]  # second row, first column, fourth layer → 20
So the dimensions c(2,3,4) describe the size of the array along each axis: rows, columns, and layers.

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
section: What is a list and what can it contain?
text:
What is a list and what can it contain?
A list is a flexible data structure in R that can store multiple elements of different types in a single object. Unlike vectors, matrices, and arrays, which must contain elements of the same type, a list can hold a mixture of data types and even other data structures.
A list can contain:

Numeric values
Character strings
Logical values
Vectors
Matrices
Data frames
Other lists (nested lists)
Functions

This makes lists very useful for storing complex or hierarchical data, such as the results of statistical models, grouped observations, or structured information about an experiment.
my_list <- list(
  name = "John",
  age = 25,
  scores = c(90,85,88)
)

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
List indexing
my_list$name
my_list[1]
my_list[[1]]
Key difference
In R, lists can be indexed in two main ways: using single brackets [ ] or double brackets [[ ]]. These two methods behave differently and return different types of results.
When you use single brackets [ ], R returns a sub-list. This means it keeps the structure of a list, even if you select only one element. In other words, [ ] filters or selects elements from the list, but the result is still a list.
Example:
my_list <- list(name = "John", age = 25, scores = c(90,85,88))

my_list[1]
This returns:
$name
[1] "John"
Even though only one element was selected, the result is still a list containing that element.
In contrast, when you use double brackets [[ ]], R extracts the actual element stored at that position. It removes the list structure and returns the object itself, in its original class.
Example:
my_list[[1]]
This returns:
[1] "John"
Now the result is a character vector, not a list.
So the key idea is:

[ ] filters the list and returns a list
[[ ]] extracts the element and returns its original class

For example:
class(my_list[1])    # "list"
class(my_list[[1]])  # "character"
This distinction is very important when working with lists, especially when you need to access the actual data inside them.



Syntax
Returns




[ ]
Sub-list


[[ ]]
Element itself


$
Named element

title: R Data Structures and Indexing
text:
Using aggregate()
data(OrchardSprays)

aggregate(
  x = OrchardSprays$decrease,
  by = list(treatment = OrchardSprays$treatment),
  FUN = mean
)
The aggregate() function is used to compute summary statistics for subsets of data. In this example, it calculates the mean of the decrease variable for each level of the treatment variable.
How it works:

x = OrchardSprays$decrease specifies the numeric variable to be summarised.
by = list(treatment = OrchardSprays$treatment) defines the grouping variable.
FUN = mean tells R to compute the mean for each group.

The result is a new data frame where each row represents a treatment group and the corresponding mean decrease.
Why use a list in by instead of a vector:
The by argument expects a list because it is designed to handle one or more grouping variables. Each element of the list represents a grouping factor. Even if there is only one grouping variable, it must still be wrapped in a list.
For example:
by = list(OrchardSprays$treatment)
If you had two grouping variables, you could write:
by = list(
  treatment = OrchardSprays$treatment,
  block = OrchardSprays$rowpos
)
Using a list allows aggregate() to create combinations of grouping variables and compute summaries for each combination. A single vector would not support multiple grouping factors in this way.

Dimensional structures

title: Data Manipulation with dplyr
text:
A Data Transformation Recipe
A recipe is:

A reproducible sequence of split–apply–combine operations that converts raw data into structured analytical output.



Structure:


Raw → Clean → Partition → Apply → Combine → Visualise

title: Data Manipulation with dplyr
section: The dplyr Pipe and Recipe Flow
text:
The dplyr Pipe and Recipe Flow
A dplyr recipe is a step-by-step transformation of data


Each stage passes its result to the next
The key ingredient for recipe flow is the pipe operator (%>% or |>) which reads as “and then.”



Allows you to express a sequence of operations that mimic your analytic reasoning:


Take raw data, and then filter, and then group, and then summarise, and then reshape.

title: Data Manipulation with dplyr
text:
Anatomy of a dplyr Recipe
A typical dplyr transformation has this sequential structure:
data %>%
  filter(...) %>%         # Step 1: Remove unwanted rows
  mutate(...) %>%         # Step 2: Add or modify columns
  group_by(...) %>%       # Step 3: Define partitions
  summarise(...) %>%      # Step 4: Aggregate within partitions
  arrange(...)            # Step 5: Order the results (optional)


Each line is a verb, describing what to do at that step.
The output of one operation becomes the input of the next.
This sequential flow matches the way you think about transforming data.

title: Data Manipulation with dplyr
text:
Anatomy of a dplyr recipe
Pipelines improve readability and reproducibility

Makes analysis transparent
Trace the journey from messy input to structured output

title: Data Manipulation with dplyr
text:
Piping it all together…
dplyr

starwars |> 
  filter(!is.na(mass)) |>         # Remove rows where mass is NA
  group_by(species) |>            # Group data by species
  summarise(avg_mass = mean(mass)) |>  # Mean mass for each species
  arrange(desc(avg_mass))         # Sort results by mean mass, descending

Base R

# Filter out NAs
filtered <- starwars[!is.na(starwars$mass), ]

# Mmean mass by species
avg_mass <- aggregate(mass ~ species, data = filtered, FUN = mean)

# Sort descending
avg_mass <- avg_mass[order(-avg_mass$mass), ]

title: Hypothesis testing

Hypotheses: Null vs Alternative

Null Hypothesis (H₀):
The assumption that there is no effect or no difference.
Example: “There is no difference in test scores between two groups.”
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁ or Ha):
The assumption that there is an effect or a difference.
Example: “There is a difference in test scores between two groups.”

title: Hypothesis testing
text:
P-value: Definition and Interpretation

P-value:
The probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as the ones observed, under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true.
Interpretation:
A small p-value (typically < 0.05) suggests that the observed data is unlikely under the null hypothesis, leading to rejection of H₀.
A large p-value suggests that the data is consistent with the null hypothesis.

1 Student’s T-test
William Sealy Gosset is credited with inventing the t-test while working for the Guinness brewery. The idea was refined and supported by the great statistician R. A. Fisher, and the idea was initially described in a paper anonymously by “Student”, in order to protect the commercial interests of Guinness. Today, it is perhaps one of the most prevalent and basic tools in statistics, and it is a fascinating story.

Graphing

Practice exercises

title: T-test
text:
2 The question of the t-test
The typical premise of the t-test is that it is used to compare populations you are interested in, which you measure with independent samples. There are a few versions of the basic question.

title: T-test
text:
Compare two independent samples

Here you have measured a numeric variable and have two samples.
Are the means of the two samples different (i.e. did the samples come from different populations)?
Example: An experiment with a control and one treatment group.

title: T-test
section: Compare 1 sample to a known mean
text:
Compare 1 sample to a known mean

Here you have one sample which you wish to compare to a mean value.
Did the sample come from a population exhibiting the known mean?
The data are simply a single numeric vector, and the population mean for comparison.

title: T-test
text:
Paired samples

Here the individual observation comprising the 2 samples are not independent.
Example: Before vs After experiments
Another example: Measuring plots that are paired spatially
For each of these examples, there is a unit, patient, or plot identification, that represents the relationship of each paired measure.

title: T-test
text:
3 Data and assumptions
The principle assumptions of the t-test are:

Gaussian distribution of observations WITHIN each sample
Heteroscedasticity (our old friend) - i.e., the variance is equal in each sample
Independence of observations

title: The Chi-Square story
text:
The Wilderness of Counts
By the early 1900s, Karl Pearson had become a towering figure in the emerging field of statistics. With his invention of correlation, regression, and his devotion to the bell-shaped curve, he had given scientists tools to understand continuous data — things like height, weight, and age. These were the triumphs of mathematical elegance: smooth curves, symmetrical relationships, and clean, interpretable numbers.
Pearson believed that data — even data from nature — could be domesticated into symmetry. The world, as he saw it, was measurable, and the key to scientific advancement was in reducing complex variation to mathematical law. The normal distribution was the centrepiece of this worldview. It wasn’t just a technical tool — it was a philosophical claim. That under the chaos of nature, there was balance. Predictability. Order.
However, in the background, something nagged him; not all data is continous. there is a lot of categorical data for which you can’t calculate a mean or do regression. how do you interrogate such data and aswer questions?
Let’s consider this hypothetical scenario and frame the rest of the story on it: One day, a naturalist came to Karl Pearson with a very interesting kind of data.

“In Glen Affric,” the naturalist explained, “I observed 30 golden eagles and 20 red kites. In Glen Nevis, 25 golden eagles and 25 red kites. In Rannoch Moor, 15 eagles and 35 kites. Are the species counts dependent on location or it doesnt matter? and at each location, do the species counts/proportions match our expectations?”

There were no heights. No weights. No means. Just categories — and counts.
This data defied Pearson’s existing tools. You cannot take the average of ‘red kite’ and ‘golden eagle’. You cannot compute a standard deviation across glens, nor fit a bell curve to discrete bird species. And yet, the question behind the data was clearly statistical: Are bird species independent of location, or is there a hidden ecological pattern?
This wasn’t idle curiosity. In an era before modern conservation policy, understanding the distribution of species across landscapes was vital. If red kites preferred moors and golden eagles favoured highland glens, it could suggest niche partitioning — or it could suggest environmental degradation, habitat competition, or even human interference.
And so Pearson found himself standing before an intellectual chasm: how do you analyse data that has no mean, no variance, no curve?

title: The Chi-Square story
text:
The Problem of Categorical Data
Pearson understood immediately what was at stake. He had built a framework that was astonishingly effective — but it had boundaries. The logic of correlation, for instance, assumed that the underlying variables were normally distributed. If not, the coefficient could be distorted, biased, even misleading. His early work relied on the assumption that nature, when measured, would fall obediently into the arms of the bell curve.
But here, in this messy field data, the bell curve had no place. The data could not be smoothed or standardised. They were counts, nothing more — frequencies of occurrence. Yet beneath those frequencies lay a pattern. The very idea of science is to determine whether a pattern is real or illusory. And so Pearson began to think.
If you couldn’t compare means, perhaps you could compare frequencies — not in the sense of variance, but in the sense of discrepancy. How different is what we observe from what we expect?
And thus emerged one of the most brilliant — and most underappreciated — shifts in modern science.

title: The Chi-Square story
section: A Test for Discrepancy: The Birth of the Chi-Square
text:
A Test for Discrepancy: The Birth of the Chi-Square
Pearson realised he needed to quantify the gap between expectation and observation. He devised a deceptively simple formula:
\[
\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}
\]

\(O_i\) was the observed count in each category.
\(E_i\) was the expected count, under the assumption of independence.
Squaring the difference removed direction — a shortfall or an excess both became evidence.
Dividing by \(E_i\) scaled the contribution of each category, adjusting for the size of expectation.

In this sum, Pearson saw a universal measure of surprise. If the observations closely matched expectations, chi-square would be small. If they diverged wildly, the statistic would grow large.
But was it meaningful? Could he say when the result was too large to have arisen by chance?
Yes — and this is where Pearson’s mathematical gift became apparent. He derived the theoretical distribution of chi-square under the null hypothesis. He showed that, when the expected frequencies were large enough and the observations were independent, the statistic followed a specific pattern — what would become known as the chi-square distribution.
It was: - Bounded below at 0 (perfect match) - Right-skewed, especially with few categories - Unbounded above — allowing for arbitrarily large mismatches, though increasingly improbable
This distribution let Pearson calculate, for any given \(X^2\) value, the probability of observing such a result under the assumption of independence.
It was a revelation. For the first time, one could assign a mathematical likelihood to a pattern in categorical data.

title: The Chi-Square story
text:
Why “Chi-Square”?
The naming was natural. Pearson used the Greek letter \(X\) to represent the variable — a common notation at the time. Since the formula involved the sum of squared discrepancies, he called it chi-square. What began as a placeholder symbol became the name of one of the most important distributions in statistics.

title: The Chi-Square story
section: The Ripple Effect: More than Independence
text:
The Ripple Effect: More than Independence
At first, the \(X^2\) test was used primarily to test goodness-of-fit and independence — such as whether bird species and habitats were associated. But over time, its versatility became apparent. It was used to:

Test fairness of dice and coins
Validate genetic segregation ratios
Detect selection bias in sampling
Analyse voting patterns

And in a particularly elegant twist, it became a way to test one of Pearson’s own assumptions: normality.
Remember: the correlation coefficient Pearson developed relies on data being approximately normal. If that assumption fails, the coefficient can behave badly — inflating or hiding relationships.
But how do you test whether data is normal? One way, Pearson realised, was to bin the data into categories — say, intervals of values — and compare the observed frequencies with the probabilities predicted by a normal distribution.
In this way, the chi-square test became a way to evaluate how well continuous data conformed to a normal model. The logic was recursive. The chi-square test could test the assumptions required for the very methods Pearson had pioneered.
It was a beautiful moment of statistical self-reflection. The tool for testing categories could be used to validate the use of tools for continuous variables.

title: The Chi-Square story
text:
Visualising the Chi-Square Distribution


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Example: chi-square with 3 degrees of freedom
df <- 3
x <- seq(0, 20, length.out = 500)
y <- dchisq(x, df = df)

ggplot(data.frame(x, y), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = qchisq(0.95, df), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = qchisq(0.95, df) + 1.2, y = 0.05,
           label = "Critical value (\u03B1 = 0.05)", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Chi-Square Distribution (df = 3)",
       x = expression(chi^2), y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()

title: The Chi-Square story
section: Demonstrating Chi-Square in R with Real Datasets
text:
Demonstrating Chi-Square in R with Real Datasets
chi-square test of independence
Let’s walk through the naturalist’s bird observations and answer the first question, that is; Are the species counts dependent on location or it doesnt matter? This requires us to test whether two categorical variables are independent (e.g., species vs location). For this, Karl came up with the chi-square test of independence, the more nuanced of two flavours of chi-square tests (we will show the other one below). It test requires us to make two-way tables as follows:
Step 1: Create the observed table


Code
bird_counts <- matrix(c(
  30, 20,  # Glen Affric
  25, 25,  # Glen Nevis
  15, 35   # Rannoch Moor
), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)

rownames(bird_counts) <- c("Glen Affric", "Glen Nevis", "Rannoch Moor")
colnames(bird_counts) <- c("Golden Eagle", "Red Kite")
bird_counts


Step 2: Get row/column totals and compute expected values
Before computing the chi-square statistic, we need the expected values — the counts we’d expect in each cell if bird species and location were independent.
You might ask:
Why aren’t expected values just evenly split, like 0.5 for each cell?
Because the overall row and column totals aren’t evenly split. The expected count for each cell depends on both:
How many total birds are at each location (row totals), and
How many total birds belong to each species (column totals)
For example:
Golden eagles make up 70 out of 150 birds → 46.7%
Red kites make up 80 out of 150 birds → 53.3%
We use these proportions to distribute expectations across each location.
\[
E_{ij} = \frac{(\text{Row Total}_i \times \text{Column Total}_j)}{\text{Grand Total}}
\]
What outer() does here is multiply each row total with each column total, producing a matrix of numerators. Then we divide each by the grand total to get expected counts under the null hypothesis of independence.
These expected values are what you’d expect if location and species are unrelated. The rest of the test compares observed counts to these expectations.


Code
row_totals <- rowSums(bird_counts)
col_totals <- colSums(bird_counts)
total <- sum(bird_counts)

expected <- outer(row_totals, col_totals) / total
expected


Step 3: Compute chi-square statistic manually


Code
chisq_contrib <- (bird_counts - expected)^2 / expected
round(chisq_contrib, 2)  # Show individual contributions

chisq_manual <- sum(chisq_contrib)
chisq_manual  # Final chi-square value


Step 4 (optional): Compare to chisq.test()


Code
chisq.test(bird_counts)


Note:  The two tests yield equal results. We showed the manual calculation just to show you what the function does underneath. Also note that Karl would have stopped at calculating the X-squared value. the p-values are a later invention.
Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test
This can help us answer the second question; At each location, do the species counts/proportions match our expectations?
This test: - Requires a single categorical variable, with expected proportions supplied

Tests whether observed counts match expected counts
No need for a two-way table; One row is fine, because we are testing whether the distribution of categories fits a given expectation at a location.

Suppose you observed just Glen Affric:


Code
observed <- c(Golden_Eagle = 30, Red_Kite = 20)
observed


Let’s say your prior ecological knowledge says:

Golden eagles should be 60%
Red kites should be 40%

Then the expected should be:


Code
expected <- c(0.6, 0.4) * sum(observed)  # 60% and 40% of 50
expected


Then the chi-square goodness-of-fit test is:


Code
chisq.test(x = observed, p = c(0.6, 0.4))

title: The Chi-Square story
text:
On the p-values
In a chi-square test, the critical value serves as a threshold beyond which the observed data is considered too unlikely to have occurred by chance, assuming the null hypothesis is true. For example, if we are testing whether a single set of bird species counts matches expected proportions using a chi-square goodness-of-fit test with two categories, the degrees of freedom would be 1. At the conventional 5% significance level (α = 0.05), the critical value from the chi-square distribution is 3.84. This means that if the calculated chi-square statistic exceeds 3.84, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the observed frequencies differ significantly from the expected ones. Conversely, if the statistic is less than or equal to 3.84, we fail to reject the null — the data are consistent with our expectations. This critical value isn’t chosen arbitrarily; it marks the point on the chi-square curve beyond which only 5% of the distribution lies. In essence, it represents the boundary of “statistical surprise”: if your data cross this boundary, the mismatch is too large to attribute to randomness alone, and thus, potentially meaningful.

title: The Chi-Square story
text:
Some real data
Let’s apply Pearson’s insight to real datasets. These examples show how we test categorical associations in modern contexts — ecology, sustainability, and applied biology.
1. mtcars: Transmission vs. Engine Cylinders (vehicle design)


Code
tab1 <- table(mtcars$cyl, mtcars$am)
knitr::kable(tab1, caption = "Contingency Table: Cylinders vs Transmission")
chisq.test(tab1)



Interpretation: Is the number of cylinders in a car independent of whether it has an automatic or manual transmission? In sustainability contexts, this may reflect the evolution of engine design towards efficiency.

title: The Chi-Square story
section: Conclusion: A Legacy Beyond the Curve
text:
Conclusion: A Legacy Beyond the Curve
Pearson began his statistical life in pursuit of curves. His early work was an ode to the normal distribution — a belief that nature followed symmetric laws. But with the chi-square test, he acknowledged something deeper: that patterns exist even in the absence of smoothness.
Where there is no mean, no variance, no regression line — there may still be structure. And where there is structure, there is science.
In testing independence, fairness, association, and normality, the chi-square test has proven to be one of the most versatile and enduring tools in the history of data. And for students and scientists alike, it offers a profound lesson:

The world may not always follow the curve — but it always leaves a trace in its frequencies.

title: Correlation Analysis
text:
The question
Correlation describes the direction and strength of association between two variables.

Positive association: larger values of one variable tend to accompany larger values of the other.
Negative association: larger values of one variable tend to accompany smaller values of the other.
Weak association: knowing one variable gives little information about the other.
Strong association: observations follow a clear increasing or decreasing pattern.

title: Correlation Analysis
text:
Start with a graph

plot(
  iris$Sepal.Length,
  iris$Petal.Length,
  pch = 19,
  col = "steelblue",
  xlab = "Sepal length",
  ylab = "Petal length",
  main = "Sepal and petal length"
)

A correlation coefficient should always be interpreted alongside a graph because unusual shapes, clusters, and outliers can be hidden by a single number.

title: Correlation Analysis
Correlation Analysis
text:
Pearson’s product-moment correlation
Pearson’s correlation coefficient, usually written as \(r\), measures the strength of a linear association.

\(r = 1\) represents a perfect positive linear relationship.
\(r = 0\) represents no linear relationship.
\(r = -1\) represents a perfect negative linear relationship.


cor(
  iris$Sepal.Length,
  iris$Petal.Length,
  method = "pearson"
)

title: Correlation Analysis
text:
Testing the association

pearson_result <- cor.test(
  iris$Sepal.Length,
  iris$Petal.Length,
  method = "pearson"
)

pearson_result

The test evaluates the null hypothesis that the population correlation is zero. Report the coefficient, confidence interval, p-value, sample size, and scientific context.

title: Correlation Analysis
text:
Interpreting magnitude
Descriptions such as weak, moderate, and strong depend on the subject area, measurement quality, and practical consequences. A modest correlation may matter greatly in one setting and have little practical relevance in another.

title: Correlation Analysis
Correlation Analysis
text:
Examine the shape

plot(
  iris$Sepal.Length,
  iris$Petal.Length,
  pch = 19,
  col = rgb(0.1, 0.3, 0.7, 0.5),
  xlab = "Sepal length",

abline(lm(Petal.Length ~ Sepal.Length, data = iris), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)

title: Correlation Analysis
text:
Groups can change the story

cols <- c("setosa" = "#1b9e77", "versicolor" = "#d95f02", "virginica" = "#7570b3")
plot(
  iris$Sepal.Length,
  iris$Petal.Length,
  pch = 19,
  col = cols[iris$Species],
  xlab = "Sepal length",
  ylab = "Petal length"
)
legend("topleft", legend = names(cols), col = cols, pch = 19, bty = "n")

The overall relationship may partly reflect differences between species, which illustrates why context and potential confounders belong in the interpretation.

title: Correlation Analysis
text:
Spearman’s rank correlation
Spearman’s coefficient measures a monotonic relationship using ranks. It is useful for ordinal variables, skewed measurements, or relationships that increase consistently without forming a straight line.

spearman_result <- cor.test(
  iris$Sepal.Length,
  iris$Petal.Length,
  method = "spearman",
  exact = FALSE
)

spearman_result

title: Correlation Analysis
text:
Kendall’s tau
Kendall’s tau is based on concordant and discordant pairs and is often useful with smaller samples or many tied ranks.

kendall_result <- cor.test(
  iris$Sepal.Length,
  iris$Petal.Length,
  method = "kendall",
  exact = FALSE
)

kendall_result
