Definition: statistical model
A statistical model is a simplified mathematical description of a real system.

It focuses on relationships between variables (and uncertainty),
not just drawing a curve through points.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Linear vs non-linear (intuition)
A relationship can be:

linear additive: a fixed change in x gives a fixed change in expected y
non-linear: diminishing returns, saturation, thresholds, etc.


Use this to motivate “linear regression is a tool, not the truth”.

text: Linear vs non-linear

title: Linear Regression
text:
“Linear” means linear in the parameters
A linear model can include transformed predictors:

✅ y = β0 + β1 x + β2 x^2 + ε is linear in β’s
✅ y = β0 + β1 log(x) + ε is linear in β’s
❌ y = β0 + exp(β1 x) + ε is not linear in β’s

title: Linear Regression
section: The linear model in matrix form
text:
The linear model in matrix form
\[
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
\]

y: response/outcome
X: design matrix (predictors encoded as columns)
β: coefficients/parameters
ε: residual error (unexplained part)

title: Linear Regression
text:
What regression is for
Simple regression often answers at least one of:

Prediction: estimate y at new x
Explanation: quantify change in y per unit x
Variance accounting: how much variation in y is associated with x
Inference: hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: Linear Regression
text:
Regression to the mean (intuition)
Regression to the mean happens when you pick people (or things) because they had an extreme result once, then measure them again.
What you see: the extreme scores move closer to average on the second measurement.
Why? Every measurement has some randomness (luck, conditions, mood, error). When you pick “the best” or “the worst” from one measurement, you accidentally pick people who got lucky (or unlucky) that day. Next time, their luck is different—so their score drifts back toward their usual level.
Key examples:

Students who bombed an exam → tend to do better on a retest (even with no extra study)
“Rookie of the year” → often has a more normal second season
Worst-performing stores → often improve next quarter (even with no intervention)

The trap: this looks like improvement (or decline), but it’s just randomness evening out. Nothing actually changed.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Why is it called “regression”?
The connection: linear regression literally models regression to the mean.
History: Francis Galton (1886) studied parent and child heights. He noticed:

Very tall parents → children are tall, but closer to average height
Very short parents → children are short, but closer to average height

He called this “regression toward mediocrity” (we now say “regression to the mean”).
Mathematics: When you fit a regression line \(\hat{y} = \alpha + \beta x\), you’re estimating the conditional mean: the average y for a given x.

If correlation is perfect (\(\rho = 1\)), the line has slope = 1 (no regression to mean)
If correlation is imperfect (\(\rho < 1\)), the line is flatter than 45°, which means extreme x values predict y values closer to the mean

So: linear regression is the mathematical tool that quantifies how much extreme values regress back toward the mean. The phenomenon gave the method its name!

title: Linear Regression
text:
Caution: correlation ≠ causation
Regression describes association in your dataset.
To talk about causality you need:

design (randomisation, controls),
or a strong causal argument (assumptions you can defend).

title: Linear Regression

The simple regression model
\[
y_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \varepsilon_i,\quad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
\]

α: intercept (expected y when x = 0)
β: slope (change in expected y for +1 in x)
ε: residual (what’s left)

title: Linear Regression
section: Where do the coefficients come from?
text:
Where do the coefficients come from?
Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
Ordinary least squares chooses alpha, beta to minimise:
\[
\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]
This is the sum of squared residuals.
Why least squares?

Squaring makes all errors positive
Larger errors are penalised more heavily
The mathematics becomes tractable (closed-form solution)

Why ordinary?
Because we assume:

all observations have equal variance
all observations are equally reliable
errors are independent

If these are not true, we move to:

Weighted least squares (different variances)
Generalised least squares (correlated errors)
Mixed models (hierarchical structure)

So “ordinary” = the simplest, default case.
Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses α, β that minimise:
\[
\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]
This is why you’ll hear “least squares line of best fit”.

title: Linear Regression
text:
R² (variance explained)
How much variation does the model explain?
Caution:

high R² ≠ causal truth
R² can increase just by adding predictors (use adjusted R², or better, validation)

title: Linear Regression
text:
p-values, confidence intervals, and power
Full model summary:
What is being tested?
For each coefficient \(\beta_j\), the null hypothesis is:
\[
H_0: \beta_j = 0
\]
The test statistic is:
\[
t = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j}{SE(\hat{\beta}_j)}
\]
This follows a t-distribution under the model assumptions.
ANOVA view of regression
ANOVA partitions variance into:

Model (Regression) sum of squares
Residual (Error) sum of squares

The F-statistic is:
\[
F = \frac{MS_{model}}{MS_{error}}
\]
If this ratio is large, the model explains much more variance than expected by chance.
Confidence intervals
A 95% CI is the range of slopes compatible with the data under the model.

How to read this

Estimate: the fitted coefficient (alpha or beta)
Std. Error: uncertainty in that estimate
t value: Estimate / Std. Error
Pr(>|t|): p-value for H0: coefficient = 0

Intercept
The intercept is the expected value of y when all predictors = 0.

Sometimes meaningful (e.g. baseline control)
Often meaningless (e.g. bill length = 0 mm is impossible)

Slope (beta)
The slope is the expected change in y per 1-unit increase in x, holding other predictors constant.
Units always matter:

g per mm, kg per ha, t per °C, etc.

With factors
Here:

One level is the reference (baseline)
Other coefficients are differences from that reference

Example interpretation:

(Intercept) = mean of reference species
speciesChinstrap = difference between Chinstrap and reference

With interactions
Model with interaction term:
Interpretation:

Main slope = effect in reference species
Interaction term = change in slope for the other species

yield ~ variety * fertiliser: how different is the yield for variety A with fertiliser B from yield for variety A with fertiliser A?


The big rule

Every coefficient is a conditional comparison.

It is always interpreted given the other terms in the model are held constant.

Core assumptions
In practice we check these assumptions about residuals:

Linearity of mean structure
Homoscedasticity (constant variance)
Independence

If you see curvature in residuals vs fitted:

Homoscedasticity: “fan” shape
If residual spread increases with fitted values:

consider transforming the response (e.g., log)
consider robust SEs (later modules), or different model family

title: Linear Regression
text:
Independence: design matters
Independence is usually not visible from a single plot.
Breaks happen with:

repeated measures (same subject multiple times)
spatial dependence
time series

If independence is violated, standard errors can be wrong → misleading p-values.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Normality: mostly about small-sample inference
Normal residuals matter most when:

sample size is small
you need accurate confidence intervals/tests

With moderate/large samples, regression is often robust, but you still diagnose.

How bias and variance trade off

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Bias vs variance – intuition

Imagine we are throwing darts at a bullseye.
The true value is the centre of the target.
Each dart is an estimate (e.g. mean from a sample).

We care about two things:

Bias: Are our darts systematically off-centre?
Variance: Are our darts tightly clustered or widely spread?

Ideally: low bias & low variance
→ darts tightly clustered around the centre.

title: Sampling Theory
text: Bullseye scenarios

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Part 2 – Sampling theory

How inference depends on your sampling design
Design-based vs model-based thinking
Error, power, and effect size

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Design-based vs model-based inference

Design-based inference: randomness comes from the sampling design (e.g., SRS, stratified, cluster).
Estimators are justified by randomization; validity does not rely on a strong model for the population.
Model-based inference: treat the population as a realization of a statistical model (e.g., spatial regression, Gaussian field).
Inference is conditional on the model being approximately correct.
In practice, design-based approaches are robust but can be inefficient, while model-based approaches can be very efficient but fragile if the model is wrong.
Many modern surveys use a hybrid strategy: a good probability design plus a model to improve precision.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Typical sampling designs (conceptual)

Simple random sampling (SRS): every unit has equal chance; conceptually simple, design-based gold standard.
Stratified sampling: partition the population into strata and sample within each; improves precision and ensures coverage.
Cluster sampling: sample whole groups (clusters) of nearby units; cheaper logistically but with larger sampling error.

title: Sampling Theory
section: How do we decide on a sample size?
text:
How do we decide on a sample size?
Determining how many samples you need is as fundamental as choosing where they should come from. In environmental science, sample size influences cost, effort, accuracy, and the credibility of your conclusions.
Sample size is driven by four quantities:

Effect size: What is the smallest meaningful difference or pattern you want to detect?
Variance: How noisy is the underlying process? More variance → larger n.
Significance level (α): Probability of a Type I error (false positive).
Power (1 − β): Probability of correctly detecting a true effect.

title: Sampling Theory
section: Type I and Type II errors
text:
Type I and Type II errors
Type I error (α)
A false positive — concluding an effect exists when it does not. We usually choose α = 0.05.
Type II error (β)
A false negative — failing to detect a real effect. Power = 1 − β measures how likely we are to detect the effect.
Typical scientific studies aim for 80% power, meaning β = 0.20.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Example: Power analysis in R
Below is an example power calculation for a two-sample t‑test when the effect size varies.

library(pwr)

effects <- seq(0.2, 1, by = 0.05)
res <- sapply(effects, function(d) pwr.t.test(d = d, power = 0.8, sig.level = 0.05, type = "two.sample")$n)

plot(effects, res, type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Effect size (Cohen's d)",
     ylab = "Required sample size per group",
     main = "Smaller effects require larger samples")

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Practical guidance

Effect size thinking matters: trivial differences do not justify massive sampling campaigns.
More variance → more samples: noisy ecological processes require deeper sampling.
Design-based sampling controls bias; model-based approaches may be more efficient if the model is correct.
Alpha and power trade-offs must be justified, not chosen arbitrarily.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Summary so far – theory
We now have: - A conceptual grounding in bias and variance - A working picture of design-based vs model-based inference - An overview of common designs: SRS, stratified, cluster - Theoretical tools for sample size, effect size, and Type I / II errors.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Convenience sampling

Convenience sampling selects units that are easiest to reach or access, rather than using random or systematic selection.
This approach is often quick and low-cost, relying on availability rather than a defined sampling plan.
It does not ensure that every member of the population has a chance of selection, introducing selection bias.
As a result, the sample may not be representative, and findings may not generalize to the broader population.
In environmental studies, examples include sampling near roads, field stations, or other easily accessible sites.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Simple random sampling (SRS)

Simple Random Sampling (SRS) is a method where every unit in the population has an equal and independent chance of being selected.
SRS does not consider spatial, temporal, or group structure—samples are chosen uniformly from the entire sampling frame.
This approach is easy to implement and provides unbiased estimates as long as all units are accessible.
It may be inefficient in populations with strong spatial structure or gradients, potentially missing some areas entirely.
SRS requires a complete list of all units and may not be practical when access or sampling is logistically constrained.


n_srs <- 20

srs_sample <- grid |>
  sample_n(n_srs)

ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = grid, aes(x, y, fill = value), color = "grey90") +
  geom_point(data = srs_sample, aes(x, y), color = "black", size = 2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = paste0("Simple random sample (n = ", n_srs, ")"), subtitle = "Unbiased under SRS", fill = "Value")

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Stratified sampling

Stratified sampling divides the population into distinct subgroups (strata) based on important characteristics (such as habitat, region, or demographic group).
Samples are randomly selected from within each stratum, ensuring that all segments of the population are represented in the final sample.
Improves precision of estimates, especially when there is substantial difference between strata but more similarity within each stratum.
The number of samples from each stratum can be proportional to its size or allocated equally, depending on study goals.
Analysis must account for stratification by appropriately weighting or aggregating results across strata to produce unbiased population-level estimates.


grid_strat <- grid |>
  mutate(
    stratum = cut(
      y,
      breaks = c(0, 3.33, 6.66, 10.1),
      labels = c("South", "Middle", "North")
    )
  )

n_per_stratum <- 8

strat_sample <- grid_strat |>
  group_by(stratum) |>
  sample_n(n_per_stratum) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = grid_strat, aes(x, y, fill = value), color = "grey90") +
  geom_point(data = strat_sample, aes(x, y, shape = stratum), color = "black", size = 2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Stratified sampling", subtitle = "Better coverage across landscape", fill = "Value", shape = "Stratum")

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Cluster sampling

Cluster sampling groups the population into clusters (e.g., spatial blocks, villages, or schools) that are often based on natural or convenient divisions.
Randomly selects entire clusters, then samples all (or a subset of) units within those chosen clusters, rather than drawing from the population at large.
Reduces cost and logistical effort, since sampling is concentrated in a small number of locations, making it practical for widely dispersed populations.
Works best when clusters are similar to each other but internally heterogeneous, so that each selected cluster is representative of the whole population.
Statistical analysis must account for the cluster structure, as observations within clusters may be more alike—this increases sampling error compared to simple random sampling.

title: Sampling Theory
section: How are clusters and strata created?
text:
How are clusters and strata created?

Clusters and strata are groupings of population units, but they differ in purpose and how they are created.

Clusters: Groups of units sampled together—often to reduce cost/logistics.
Strata: Groups of units that are internally similar, used to ensure groups are represented in the sample.


The definition of clusters or strata can greatly impact the results of sampling—so, how do we create them?

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Judgemental (Subjective) Approaches

Expert knowledge: Clusters or strata are defined by people who know the study area well (e.g., separating neighbourhoods by known boundaries, land use, or socio-economic status).
Administrative boundaries: Using counties, postal codes, schools, etc.
Pro: Fast and accessible; uses existing groupings.
Con: Can introduce bias, as groupings may not reflect underlying variation.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Model-based & Data-driven Approaches

Use of auxiliary data (e.g., satellite data, previous surveys, environmental layers) to identify groups that are similar or different.
Spatial models: Delineate regions based on predicted values from spatial models (e.g., soil properties, health metrics).
Pro: Can tailor clusters/strata to variation in the variable of interest.
Con: Requires sufficient, relevant data and analysis.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Statistical Methods – Example: k-means Clustering

k-means is an algorithm that partitions units into (k) clusters so that units within a cluster are more similar to each other than to those in other clusters.
Steps:

Specify number of clusters ((k)).
Randomly assign initial cluster centers.
Assign each unit to the nearest center.
Update centers and repeat until stable.

Application: Often used to create clusters or strata using continuous auxiliary variables (e.g., income, environmental gradients).

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Comparison: Choosing a Method

Judgemental methods: Simple, transparent, but can miss important variation.
Model-based groupings: Potentially more representative, but require good covariate data.
Statistical clustering (e.g., k-means): Objective, reproducible, works for multi-variate data, but needs careful selection of variables.


The best approach depends on your study’s goals, available data, and logistical constraints.

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Aims for this session
In this session we will:

Revisit the null (H₀) and alternative (H₁) hypotheses.
Explain what a p-value is (and is not).
Understand the role of sample size (N).
Make sense of degrees of freedom (d.f.) across different tests.
Learn how to report results clearly (in a way that works for R and other software).

title: Data and the scientific process
section: What does a statistical test give you?
text:
What does a statistical test give you?
Most basic statistical tests return three key things:

A test statistic

Correlation: r (strength + direction of linear relationship).

t-test: t (how many standard errors apart the means are).

Chi-square test: χ² (how far observed counts are from expected counts).

A p-value

A number between 0 and 1; we compare it to a chosen cut-off, often 0.05.

Degrees of freedom (d.f.) and sample size (N)

These tell you how much information went into the test.

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Some guy behind the p-value

Every statistic was defined by some single-lettered guy (\(t\), \(F\), \(r\), etc.) who repeatedly calculated it under ‘normal’, ‘mundane’ conditions that we call \(H_0\), and figured out that it forms a distribution.

P-values just find where your value falls in the range of that distribution.

If it falls way out at the edges, then it is a rare value.
It deviates from the mundane and begs us to consider the alternative \(H_1\).

2-tailed vs 1-tailed

2-tailed: We care if the value is extreme in either direction (too high or too low).
1-tailed: We only care if it’s extreme in one specific direction.

Testing Normality
Every statistical test follows this pattern, but see, the assumption is that you have otherwise normal mundane conditions, not a twisted situation, hence the focus on testing normality.

title: Data and the scientific process
section: Example question: does fertiliser affect yield?
text:
Example question: does fertiliser affect yield?
We might ask:

Is there a relationship between yield and fertiliser application rate?

We collect data on fertiliser (kg/ha) and yield (t/ha) for a number of plots and create a scatterplot.

Each dot is a plot.
The question: as fertiliser increases, does yield tend to increase, decrease, or stay the same?

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Null and alternative hypotheses (correlation example)
For this example:

Null hypothesis (H₀):
There is no linear relationship between yield and fertiliser rate in the population.
Alternative hypothesis (H₁):
There is a linear relationship between yield and fertiliser rate.

Graphically, H₀ says: if we looked at all possible plots in the population, the cloud of points would show no systematic trend – just randomness around a flat line.
H₁ says: in the population, as fertiliser changes, yield tends to move up or down consistently (positive or negative slope).

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Interpreting the p-value (big picture)
The p-value answers the question:

If the null hypothesis were true, how likely is it that we would see a result this extreme (or more extreme) just by chance in our sample?

For correlation:

If H₀ is true (no relationship), then the correlation in the population is 0.
You could still get a non-zero sample correlation just by random variation.
The p-value tells you how surprising your observed r would be under H₀.

Typical rule of thumb:

If p ≤ 0.05, we say the result is statistically significant and we reject H₀.
If p > 0.05, the result is not statistically significant; we do not have enough evidence to reject H₀.

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Example output: strong correlation
Suppose our analysis gives:

r = 0.86
p < 0.001
N = 16

Interpretation:

Strength & direction: r = 0.86 is a strong positive correlation.
p < 0.001: if there were truly no relationship in the population, seeing a correlation this strong (or stronger) in a sample of 16 by chance is extremely unlikely.
We reject H₀ and conclude there is evidence of a real positive relationship between fertiliser rate and yield.

In R, you’d see:

Pearson Correlation = .860
Sig. (2-tailed) = .000
N = 16

title: Data and the scientific process
section: Why sample size matters for p-values
text:
Why sample size matters for p-values
Imagine a very large population of insects where body size and number of eggs are not related at all (H₀ true). Now we take random samples from that population.

The left panel shows the null population: a cloud of points with no trend.
The right panels show two possible random samples (each with N = 12) from this population.

Even if the true relationship is zero, some samples will look slightly positive, some slightly negative, just by chance.

title: Data and the scientific process
section: Degrees of Freedom: The Core Idea
text:
Degrees of Freedom: The Core Idea
When we estimate the sample mean, we impose the rule that the deviations from that mean must sum to zero:
\[
\sum (x_i - \bar{x}) = 0
\]
This constraint removes one independent direction in which the data could have varied.
The sample no longer behaves like (N) independent draws from a random process. It behaves like (N-1).
Because variance measures how much free randomness is in the system, it must divide by (N-1), not (N), to reflect the correct amount of independent information.

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Emphasis!
Look at this formula for sample variance:
\[
s^2 = \frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2
\]
Remember, (N-1) just means;

Once \(\bar{x}\) is fixed, the deviations \((x_i - \bar{x})\) must sum to zero for \(\bar{x}\) to be the sample mean.
So if you give me N−1 random deviations, the last one is fixed because it has to make the sum zero so the mean comes out right.
That means the data only have N−1 truly independent directions to vary in.
Because variance is supposed to measure how much independent variability there is, the formula must also use N−1 in its denominator to match the actual degrees of freedom in the data

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Example
Suppose I tell you: “I have 5 numbers, and their mean is 5.6”.

You can pick the first number to be anything (e.g., 1). It is free to vary.
You can pick the second (e.g., 3).
You can pick the third (e.g., 5).
You can pick the fourth (e.g., 9).

But for the fifth number, you have no choice.

If the mean is 5.6, the sum must be 28.
The sum of the first four is \(1+3+5+9 = 18\).
The last number must be 10 (\(28 - 18\)).

Because we calculated the mean from the data, we used up one degree of freedom. We have \(N-1\) (i.e., 4) independent choices left.
The more parameters you fix, the more degrees of freedom you use up

title: Data and the scientific process
section: Why This Affects the t-Distribution (and others)
text:
Why This Affects the t-Distribution (and others)

The t-distribution adjusts its shape based on the degrees of freedom.
With fewer degrees of freedom, there is more sampling uncertainty, so the distribution develops heavier tails.
This means a t-value must be more extreme to be considered rare and reach a conventional threshold like (p < 0.05).
As degrees of freedom grow, the uncertainty shrinks, and the t-distribution collapses toward the normal, making evidence easier to detect.

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Why Care?

Degrees of freedom tell us how much independent information was truly available after estimating parameters.
They directly determine how strong your test statistic must be before you can claim evidence against a null hypothesis.
Fewer degrees of freedom → more doubt → stricter thresholds.
More degrees of freedom → less doubt → tighter inference.

title: Data and the scientific process
section: Chi-square test of association: example table
text:
Chi-square test of association: example table
Consider a questionnaire completed by 95 students about their mode of transport to university:




Car
Bus
Foot
Row total




Male
17
18
21
56


Female
24
8
7
39


Column total
41
26
28
95



Question:

Is there an association between gender and mode of transport?


H₀: Gender and mode of transport are independent (no association).
H₁: They are associated (e.g. males and females favour different modes).

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Chi-square test: degrees of freedom
For a chi-square test of association in an r × c table:
[ = (r - 1)(c - 1) ]
In our example:

Rows: Male, Female → r = 2
Columns: Car, Bus, Foot → c = 3

So:
[ = (2 - 1)(3 - 1) = 1 = 2. ]
Interpretation:

Once you know the row totals, column totals, and (r − 1)(c − 1) of the cells, the remaining cells are determined (they’re not free to vary independently).
The degrees of freedom count how many cells can vary freely while keeping row and column totals fixed.

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Chi-square, d.f. and p-values
Chi-square test statistics are compared to a chi-square distribution that depends on d.f.:

If your test has d.f. = 2, the critical value at p = 0.05 is about 5.99.
If your observed χ² is larger than this, p < 0.05 and you reject H₀.

R does this comparison for you and reports:

The χ² statistic.
The d.f..
The p-value (Asymp. Sig. (2-sided)).

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Reporting a Chi-square test
A clear reporting sentence includes:

The test statistic (χ²).
The degrees of freedom.
The p-value.
The sample size.

Example:

There was a significant association between gender and mode of transport
(χ² = 8.34, d.f. = 2, p < 0.02, N = 95).

If p had been ≥ 0.05, we would conclude:

There was no evidence of an association between gender and mode of transport
(χ² = …, d.f. = 2, p = …, N = 95).

title: Data and the scientific process
section: Putting it together: what to look for in output
text:
Putting it together: what to look for in output
For almost any test you run (correlation, t-test, ANOVA, chi-square), R output will always give you:

A test statistic (r, t, F, χ², etc.).
Degrees of freedom (df).
A p-value (Sig.).
The sample size (N), either in the same table or elsewhere.

When reading output:

Check p first:

If p < 0.05, you have evidence against H₀ → “statistically significant”.
If p ≥ 0.05, you do not have enough evidence to reject H₀.

Then interpret the effect:

For mean differences (t-tests): which group has the higher mean and by how much.

Report everything clearly in a sentence or two, including test statistic, d.f., p and N.

title: Data and the scientific process
text:
Summary

A statistical test always returns:

A test statistic (r, t, F, χ², …)
A p-value
Degrees of freedom and/or sample size N

P-values tell us how surprising our data are if the null hypothesis is true.
Degrees of freedom measure how many pieces of information are free to vary:

Often N − 1 (variance, one-sample t-tests).

title: The t-Test
text:
What this session is about
By the end of this session, you should be able to explain:

why a sampling distribution matters
what a z-score is doing
why the t-statistic looks like a z-score
what the t-distribution actually represents
why the t-distribution depends on degrees of freedom
how p-values and critical values come from areas under the curve

title: The t-Test
section: You mostly ever see one sample
text:
You mostly ever see one sample
In real research, you do not observe the whole population.
You observe one sample.
That sample gives you one sample mean:
\[
\bar{x}
\]
But your sample was only one possible sample.
If you had repeated the study, you would probably have obtained a slightly different mean.

title: The t-Test
text:
The first big idea

A sample statistic is not fixed.
It varies from sample to sample.
So when we calculate a sample mean, we focus on this idea:

Random sampling produces a range of possible sample means.

That question leads to the idea of a sampling distribution.

title: The t-Test
section: A sampling distribution is a distribution of statistics
text:
A sampling distribution is a distribution of statistics
Imagine repeating the same study many times.
Each time:

take a sample
calculate the sample mean
store that sample mean

After many repetitions, you would have a distribution of sample means.
That is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\).

title: The t-Test
text:
Simulating a sampling distribution

population <- rnorm(100000, mean = 100, sd = 15)
sample_means <- replicate(
  5000,
  mean(sample(population, size = 25, replace = TRUE))
)
sampling_df <- data.frame(sample_mean = sample_means)
ggplot(sampling_df, aes(x = sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 45) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(population), linewidth = 1) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    title = "A sampling distribution of sample means",
    x = "Sample mean",
    y = "Density"
  )

title: The t-Test
text:
The meaning of this plot

The x-axis shows possible sample means.
The y-axis shows probability density: where sample means tend to concentrate.
The centre is close to the true population mean.
The spread tells us how much the sample mean varies from sample to sample.

title: The t-Test
text:
Standard error
Sample means have less variance than individual observation statistics.
If the population standard deviation is \(\sigma\), then the standard deviation of the sample mean is:
\[
SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
This is called the standard error. Technically we should use the sample standard deviation, but it is often approximated by the population standard deviation.
Remember: Standard in standard error just means the numerator is normalised by
It measures the expected sampling variability of \(\bar{x}\).

title: The t-Test
text:
The z-statistic
If the population standard deviation is known, we can calculate:
\[
Z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}
\]
This tells us how many standard errors the sample mean is away from \(\mu\).

title: The t-Test
text:
The hidden assumption

The z-statistic assumes that \(\sigma\) is known.
That is a very strong assumption.
In many real experiments, especially small experiments, we do not know the population standard deviation.

We estimate it from the same sample:
\[
s
\]
This changes everything.

title: The t-Test
text:
The t-statistic
When \(\sigma\) is unknown, we replace it with \(s\):
\[
t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}}
\]
This looks almost identical to a z-statistic but it is not the same object.
The denominator now contains an estimate from the data.

title: The t-Test
text:
You only calculate one t-statistic
In practice, you do not calculate a whole distribution.
You calculate one number:
\[
t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}}
\]
Then you evaluate this claim:

This value may be unusual relative to what we would expect if the null hypothesis were true.

To answer that, you need a reference distribution.
That reference distribution is the t-distribution.

title: The t-Test
section: The t-distribution as a thought experiment
text:
The t-distribution as a thought experiment
The t-distribution is the distribution of t-statistics you would get if you repeated the same experiment many times under the null hypothesis.
Each repetition would produce a new sample.
Each sample would produce:

a sample mean \(\bar{x}\)
a sample standard deviation \(s\)
a t-statistic

The distribution of those t-statistics is the t-distribution.

title: The t-Test
The t-Test
text:
A simulated t-distribution

n <- 5
df <- n - 1
ggplot(t_df_5, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, args = list(df = df), linewidth = 1) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    title = "A simulated t-distribution",
    subtitle = paste0("n = ", n, ", df = ", df),
    x = "Possible t-statistic values",
    y = "Density"
  )

title: The t-Test
text:
The x-axis
The x-axis contains possible values of the t-statistic.
For example:
-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3

A value near 0 means the sample mean is close to the null value.
A large positive value means the sample mean is far above the null value.
A large negative value means the sample mean is far below the null value.

title: The t-Test
text:
The y-axis

The y-axis is probability density.
It is not probability by itself.
Probability comes from area under the curve.
The total area under the whole t-distribution is 1.
That represents all possible t-statistic values.

title: The t-Test
text:
Where your t-statistic goes

After calculating your t-statistic, you place it on the x-axis.
If it lands near the centre, it is ordinary under the null hypothesis.
If it lands far into a tail, it is unusual under the null hypothesis.
The test asks how much area lies beyond your observed value.

title: The t-Test
text:
Degrees of freedom
For a one-sample t-test:
\[
df = n - 1
\]
The degrees of freedom are linked to how much independent information remains for estimating the sample variance.
Once the sample mean is estimated, the deviations from the mean are constrained to sum to zero.
That leaves \(n - 1\) freely varying deviations.

title: The t-Test
text:
Why df changes the shape

The t-statistic uses \(s\), not \(\sigma\).
When \(n\) is small, \(s\) is a noisy estimate of the true standard deviation.
Sometimes \(s\) is too large.
Sometimes \(s\) is too small.
When \(s\) is too small, the t-statistic can become very large.
That makes extreme t-values more common.

title: The t-Test
text:
Heavy tails

Small degrees of freedom produce heavier tails.
This means the distribution expects more extreme t-statistics.
It is more cautious because the denominator is uncertain.
As degrees of freedom increase, \(s\) becomes more stable.
The t-distribution gradually approaches the normal distribution.

title: The t-Test
text:
Comparing different degrees of freedom

x_vals <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 500)
compare_df <- data.frame(
  x = x_vals,
  `df = 2` = dt(x_vals, df = 2),
  `df = 5` = dt(x_vals, df = 5),
  `df = 30` = dt(x_vals, df = 30),
  `Normal` = dnorm(x_vals)
) |>
  pivot_longer(-x, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "density")
ggplot(compare_df, aes(x = x, y = density, colour = distribution)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    title = "The t-distribution changes with degrees of freedom",
    x = "Possible t-statistic values",
    y = "Density",
    colour = "Distribution"
  )

title: The t-Test
text:
The important interpretation

A t-value of 2 does not always mean the same thing.
It depends on the degrees of freedom.
With low df, a t-value of 2 is less surprising because the distribution is wider.
With high df, a t-value of 2 is more surprising because the distribution is tighter.
That is why the t-test must know the df.

title: The t-Test
text:
Probability comes from area

The curve gives density.
The area under the curve gives probability.
Once we calculate a t-statistic, we make this area-based interpretation:

The area beyond this value determines how unusual it is under the null model.

That area is the basis of the p-value.

title: The t-Test
text:
Right-tail area

observed_t <- 1.86
df <- 9
right_tail <- 1 - pt(observed_t, df = df)
right_tail

This is the probability of getting a t-statistic at least this large under the null hypothesis.

title: The t-Test
text:
Left-tail area

left_tail <- pt(-observed_t, df = df)
left_tail

This is the probability of getting a t-statistic this small or smaller under the null hypothesis.

title: The t-Test
text:
Two-tailed area

two_tailed <- 2 * (1 - pt(abs(observed_t), df = df))
two_tailed

This is the probability of getting a t-statistic at least this extreme in either direction.
This is the usual p-value for a two-tailed t-test.

title: The t-Test
text:
Visualising the observed t-statistic

plot_df <- data.frame(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 500)) |>
  mutate(density = dt(x, df = df))
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = x, y = density)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_t, linewidth = 1) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    title = "Place your observed t-statistic on the t-distribution",
    subtitle = paste0("Observed t = ", observed_t, ", df = ", df),
    x = "t-statistic",
    y = "Density"
  )

title: The t-Test
section: Going backwards from area to cutoff
text:
Going backwards from area to cutoff
Sometimes we choose the area first.
For example, in a two-tailed test with:
\[
\alpha = 0.05
\]
we place 2.5% of the area in the left tail and 2.5% in the right tail.
The t-values that mark those tail boundaries are called critical values.

title: The t-Test
text:
Calculating a two-tailed critical value

alpha <- 0.05
df <- 9
t_critical <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df = df)
t_critical

For \(df = 9\), the two-tailed 5% critical values are:
\[
-t^* \quad \text{and} \quad +t^*
\]

title: The t-Test
text:
Visualising critical values

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = x, y = density)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-t_critical, t_critical), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_t, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    title = "Critical values create rejection regions",
    subtitle = paste0("Two-tailed alpha = ", alpha, ", df = ", df),
    x = "t-statistic",
    y = "Density"
  )

title: The t-Test
section: How to interpret the critical values
text:
How to interpret the critical values
If the observed t-statistic is beyond the critical value, it falls into a region we agreed to treat as unusually extreme.
For a two-tailed test:
\[
|t| > t^*
\]
means reject the null hypothesis.
If the observed t-statistic is inside the critical boundaries, we do not reject the null hypothesis.

title: The t-Test
text:
One-tailed critical values
For a right-tailed test with \(\alpha = 0.05\), all 5% of the rejection area is placed in the right tail.

qt(0.95, df = 9)

This cutoff is smaller than the two-tailed cutoff because the rejection area is concentrated in one tail.

title: The t-Test
text:
Suppose we have these values
\[
\bar{x} = 101.3
\]
\[
\mu_0 = 100
\]
\[
s = 2.2
\]
\[
n = 10
\]
We test whether the true mean differs from 100.

title: The t-Test
text:
Calculate the t-statistic

xbar <- 101.3
mu0 <- 100
s <- 2.2
n <- 10
t_stat <- (xbar - mu0) / (s / sqrt(n))
t_stat

title: The t-Test
text:
Compare with the critical value

df <- n - 1
t_critical <- qt(0.975, df = df)
abs(t_stat) > t_critical

The observed t-statistic is not beyond the two-tailed critical value.
So we do not reject the null hypothesis at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

title: The t-Test
text:
Calculate the p-value

p_value <- 2 * (1 - pt(abs(t_stat), df = df))
p_value

This p-value is the two-tailed area beyond the observed t-statistic.

title: The t-Test
text:
One-sample t-test
The one-sample t-test compares one sample mean to a reference value.
You use it when:

you have one group of observations
you want to test against a known or hypothesised population mean \(\mu_0\)
population standard deviation is unknown and estimated by \(s\)

The test statistic is:
\[
t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}
\]
Interpretation:

numerator = observed difference from the null value
denominator = estimated standard error of the sample mean
large absolute t-values indicate stronger disagreement with the null model

title: The t-Test
text:
Two-sample t-test (independent groups)
The two-sample t-test compares the means of two independent groups.
You use it when:

each observation belongs to only one group
groups represent different people, units, or experimental conditions
you want to test whether \(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0\) (or another specified difference)

A common formulation is:
\[
t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}
\]
This is the usual form when the null difference is 0.
Interpretation:

the numerator is the observed mean gap
the denominator is the estimated uncertainty in that gap
inference depends on the standard error model (equal-variance or unequal-variance)

title: The t-Test
text:
Paired t-test (dependent observations)
The paired t-test is a one-sample t-test on within-pair differences.
You use it when:

each subject is measured twice (before/after)
observations are naturally matched pairs (twins, matched controls, repeated measures)
dependence exists within pairs and must be preserved in the analysis

Define the pairwise difference:
\[
d_i = x_{i,\text{before}} - x_{i,\text{after}}
\]
Then test:
\[
t = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d / \sqrt{n}}
\]
Interpretation:

the unit of analysis is the difference, not each raw measurement separately
pairing often reduces noise by removing stable person-level variability
smaller noise in differences can increase power

title: The t-Test
section: Choosing among one-sample, two-sample, and paired designs
text:
Choosing among one-sample, two-sample, and paired designs
Use this quick logic:

one-sample: one group compared with a benchmark
two-sample: two independent groups compared with each other
paired: two measurements per unit, analysed via differences

The design determines the correct t-test.
Choosing the wrong design usually gives the wrong standard error and invalid inference.

title: The t-Test
text:
Core assumptions
All t-tests rely on structural assumptions:

data values (or pairwise differences) are sampled independently
measurements are on a continuous or near-continuous scale
extreme outliers do not dominate mean and standard deviation estimates

When sample sizes are moderate or large, t-tests are often robust to mild non-normality.

title: The t-Test
text:
Distributional assumption
For small samples, the relevant analysis unit should be approximately normal:

one-sample t-test: raw values in the single group
paired t-test: within-pair differences
two-sample t-test: each group distribution should be reasonably well-behaved

Perfect normality is not required, but severe skewness plus very small \(n\) weakens reliability.

title: The t-Test
section: Equal-variance assumption for the pooled two-sample test
text:
Equal-variance assumption for the pooled two-sample test
The classical pooled two-sample t-test assumes:
\[
\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2
\]
If this is badly violated, pooled standard errors and p-values can be misleading.
That is why the unequal-variance version is often preferred in practice.

title: The t-Test
section: Practical diagnostics before running a t-test
text:
Practical diagnostics before running a t-test
Useful checks include:

inspect boxplots or histograms for strong skew and outliers
verify study design supports independence
confirm whether data are paired or independent before choosing the test
compare group spreads in two-sample settings

Diagnostics guide model choice; they do not replace domain judgement.

title: The t-Test
text:
Why Welch’s test exists
When two groups have different variances, forcing a pooled variance can distort inference.
Welch’s t-test avoids this by estimating the standard error without assuming equal variances.
It is the default for t.test(x, y) in R.

title: The t-Test
text:
Welch test statistic
Welch uses:
\[
t = \frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}
\]
with an approximate degrees-of-freedom formula (Welch-Satterthwaite).
The df can be non-integer, and that is expected.

title: The t-Test
text:
Pooled versus Welch in practice
Pooled two-sample t-test is appropriate only when equal variances are genuinely plausible.
Welch’s test is usually safer because:

it remains valid when variances differ
it performs similarly when variances are actually equal
it better handles unequal sample sizes combined with unequal variances

For most applied work, Welch should be the default independent two-sample t-test.

title: The t-Test
text:
R syntax for both versions

# Welch two-sample t-test (default)
setosa_demo <- iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "setosa"]
versicolor_demo <- iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "versicolor"]
t.test(setosa_demo, versicolor_demo)

# Pooled two-sample t-test (equal variances forced)
t.test(setosa_demo, versicolor_demo, var.equal = TRUE)

The key difference is var.equal = TRUE.
If you do not set it, R performs Welch’s test.

title: The t-Test
text:
Exercise 1 - the one sample t-test
You are a researcher studying the effect of a new drug on blood pressure.
You have a sample of 10 patients with a mean blood pressure of 120 mmHg.
The sample standard deviation is 10 mmHg.
Test whether the true mean blood pressure is different from 110 mmHg.

title: The t-Test
text:
Exercise 2 - the two sample t-test
Use the iris dataset to compare the mean petal length between the species setosa and versicolor. Test whether there is a significant difference between the two means.

# Subset Petal.Length for setosa and versicolor
setosa_petal <- iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "setosa"]
versicolor_petal <- iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "versicolor"]

# Perform a two-sample t-test (assume equal variance for now)
t_test_result <- t.test(setosa_petal, versicolor_petal, var.equal = TRUE)
t_test_result

The above output summarizes the two-sample t-test comparing Petal Length between setosa and versicolor.

Null hypothesis: The population means of Petal Length for setosa and versicolor are equal.
Alternative hypothesis: The population means are different.

Interpret the p-value: - If the p-value < 0.05, there is a significant difference between the means. - If the p-value ≥ 0.05, there is no significant difference.

title: The t-Test
text: Exercise 3 - the paired t-test

title: The t-Test
text:
Exercise 3 - the paired t-test
A nutritionist wants to test whether a new dietary supplement has an effect on cholesterol levels. She measures the cholesterol levels of 8 patients before and after using the supplement for 2 months.
The results (in mg/dL) are as follows:



Patient
Before
After




1
210
200


2
225
218


3

4

Test whether the supplement has a significant effect on mean cholesterol levels.
1. Enter the data and perform a paired t-test

# Before and after cholesterol levels
before <- c(210, 225, 240, 199, 220, 215, 230, 205)
after <- c(200, 218, 230, 192, 210, 203, 220, 202)

# Perform paired t-test
paired_ttest <- t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)
paired_ttest

2. Interpretation

Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): The mean difference in cholesterol levels (before - after) is zero (the supplement has no effect).
Alternative hypothesis (\(H_A\)): The mean difference is not zero (the supplement has an effect).

Interpret the p-value from the output:

If the p-value < 0.05, conclude that the supplement has a statistically significant effect on cholesterol levels.
If the p-value ≥ 0.05, there is no significant evidence of an effect.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
The problem chi-square solves
Many statistical tests are built for measurements.
Examples: height, yield, temperature, rainfall, body mass, exam score.
For these, means and differences between means make sense.

But many datasets are counts in categories.
Examples: pass/fail, healthy/diseased, species, location by species, treatment response.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
section: Categorical data need a different question
text:
Categorical data need a different question
For categorical counts, the average category is usually not meaningful.
The mean of healthy, infected, and dead is not a biological quantity.
Instead, we ask:

Are the counts we observed close to the counts we expected?

That is the central idea behind the chi-square test.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
The core intuition
The chi-square test is a test of discrepancy.
It compares:
Observed counts
against:
Expected counts under a null hypothesis
The test asks:

If the null hypothesis were true, would this mismatch be ordinary or surprising?

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
The hypothesis-testing logic
The chi-square test follows a familiar pattern.

State a null hypothesis.
Work out what the null hypothesis predicts.
Compare observed counts with expected counts.
Ask whether the mismatch is large relative to chance variation.

The data type is different from a t-test, but the logic is the same.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
section: A first example: rolling a die
text:
A first example: rolling a die
Suppose we roll a six-sided die 60 times.
If the die is fair, each face has probability 1/6.
So the expected count for each face is:

60 * (1/6)

[1] 10


So, under fairness, each face is expected about 10 times.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Mild mismatch



Face
Observed
Expected if fair




1
8
10


2
12
10


3
11
10


4
9

5

6

10



The observed counts are not exactly equal to expected counts.
That is normal. Random data rarely match expectation perfectly.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
The chi-square statistic
Pearson’s chi-square statistic is:
χ² = sum of (Observed − Expected)² / Expected
or more compactly:
χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E
where:

O is an observed count
E is an expected count
Σ means add over categories or table cells

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Why observed minus expected?
O − E is the raw difference between what we saw and what the null hypothesis predicted.
If we expected 10 but observed 12, the difference is +2.
If we expected 10 but observed 8, the difference is −2.
Both are mismatches of size 2, but in opposite directions.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Why square the difference?
The formula uses (O − E)².
Squaring does two things.

It removes the sign.
It gives large mismatches more weight.

For example:

2² = 4
8² = 64

A difference of 8 contributes much more than a difference of 2.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Why divide by expected?
The formula divides by E.
The same raw difference can mean different things at different scales.
A difference of 5 is huge when the expected count is 2.
A difference of 5 is tiny when the expected count is 500.
So chi-square measures mismatch relative to expectation.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Scale example
If expected = 2 and observed = 7:
(7 − 2)² / 2 = 12.5
If expected = 500 and observed = 505:
(505 − 500)² / 500 = 0.05
Both have a raw difference of 5.
Only the first is strongly surprising relative to expectation.

die <- tibble(

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
From statistic to distribution
A chi-square statistic is always zero or positive.
It cannot be negative because it is built from squared differences.
The smallest possible value is 0.
That happens when every observed count exactly equals its expected count.
But a statistic alone is not enough.
We need to know whether the statistic is large relative to chance.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
The chi-square distribution
The chi-square distribution is the reference distribution for chi-square tests.
It answers:

If the null hypothesis were true, what chi-square values would we expect from random sampling variation?

There is not just one chi-square curve.
There is a family of curves controlled by degrees of freedom.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Degrees of freedom
Degrees of freedom describe how many values are free to vary after constraints have been imposed.
For a goodness-of-fit test with k categories:
df = k − 1
For a two-way table with r rows and c columns:
df = (r − 1)(c − 1)

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Chi-square distributions

x <- seq(0, 25, length.out = 500)
chisq_curves <- expand.grid(
  x = x,
  df = c(1, 2, 5, 10)
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(density = dchisq(x, df = df))

ggplot(chisq_curves, aes(x = x, y = density, colour = factor(df))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Chi-square distributions with different degrees of freedom",
    x = "Chi-square value",
    y = "Density",
    colour = "df"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
What degrees of freedom change
As degrees of freedom increase, the distribution shifts to the right and becomes more spread out.
That makes sense.
With more categories or more table cells, there are more opportunities for random discrepancies to accumulate.
So a chi-square value that is large for 1 df may not be large for 10 df.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
The p-value
Once we have a chi-square statistic and degrees of freedom, we calculate a p-value.
The p-value asks:

If the null hypothesis were true, how often would we see a chi-square statistic at least as large as the one we observed?

A small p-value means the mismatch is unusual under the null hypothesis.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
P-value as a right-tail area

observed_chi <- chi_suspicious
df_die <- 5
x <- seq(0, 40, length.out = 1000)
plot_data <- tibble(
  x = x,
  density = dchisq(x, df = df_die),
  tail = x >= observed_chi
)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = x, y = density)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(plot_data, tail), fill = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_chi, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "The p-value is the right-tail area",
    subtitle = paste0("Observed chi-square = ", round(observed_chi, 2), ", df = ", df_die),
    x = "Chi-square value",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
A common p-value warning
The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
It is the probability of a statistic this extreme, or more extreme, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
The p-value is about the data under a model.
It is not the probability that the model is true.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Test 1: goodness-of-fit
The chi-square goodness-of-fit test is used when we have:

one categorical variable
observed counts across categories
a proposed expected distribution

It asks:

Do the observed category counts fit the expected distribution?

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Goodness-of-fit hypotheses
Null hypothesis:

The observed counts follow the expected distribution.

Alternative hypothesis:

The observed counts do not follow the expected distribution.

For a fair die:

Each face has probability 1/6.

The alternative says at least one face has a probability different from 1/6.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Expected counts for goodness-of-fit
For category i:
Expected count = total sample size × expected probability
For a fair die with 60 rolls:
Expected count = 60 × 1/6 = 10
This is why each face has expected count 10.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Goodness-of-fit in R

chisq.test(suspicious_die$observed, p = rep(1/6, 6))


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  suspicious_die$observed
X-squared = 39.4, df = 5, p-value = 1.973e-07


This compares observed counts with the counts expected under a fair die.
A low p-value suggests the observed data are not consistent with the fair-die model.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Interpreting goodness-of-fit
A significant goodness-of-fit test tells us:

The observed distribution differs from the expected distribution.

It does not prove why.
Possible explanations include:

the die is physically biased
the rolling process is biased
the data were recorded incorrectly
the rolls were not independent

Statistics detects the mismatch. Science explains the mismatch.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Test 2: independence
The chi-square test of independence is used when we have:

two categorical variables
counts in a contingency table

It asks:

Are the two categorical variables associated, or are they independent?

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Example: species and location

birds <- matrix(
  c(38, 12,
    24, 26,
    8, 42),
  nrow = 3,
  byrow = TRUE
)

rownames(birds) <- c("Glen Affric", "Glen Nevis", "Rannoch Moor")
colnames(birds) <- c("Golden Eagle", "Red Kite")

kable(birds)

Question:

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Independence hypotheses
Null hypothesis:

The two categorical variables are independent.

Alternative hypothesis:

The two categorical variables are associated.

For the bird example:

Species and location are independent.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
What independence means
Independence means that knowing one variable does not change the distribution of the other.
For the bird example:

The proportion of Golden Eagles and Red Kites should be roughly the same in each location.

If species proportions differ strongly by location, that suggests association.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Expected counts for independence
For a cell in a two-way table:
Expected count = row total × column total / grand total
This gives the count expected if the row variable and column variable were independent.
Expected counts preserve the row totals and column totals.

The p-value tells us how unusual that mismatch would be if species and location were independent.

birds_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(birds)) |>

Goodness-of-fit versus independence








Feature
Goodness-of-fit

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Simulation gives the intuition
The chi-square distribution can feel abstract.
Simulation makes it concrete.
Imagine the null hypothesis is true.
Then:

Generate many fake datasets under the null.
Calculate χ² for each fake dataset.
Ask how often fake datasets are as extreme as the observed dataset.

That is the p-value in action.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Assumptions: why they matter
Chi-square tests are simple and useful.
But they rely on assumptions.
If the assumptions are badly violated, the p-value may be misleading.
The main assumptions are about:

the type of data
category structure
independence of observations
expected counts
study design

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Assumption 1: data are counts
Chi-square tests are for counts in categories.
They are not for raw percentages, proportions, means, or continuous measurements.
This is suitable:



Outcome
Count




Healthy
42


Diseased
18



A percentage alone loses sample size.
70% of 10 and 70% of 10,000 carry very different evidence.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Assumption 2: categories are mutually exclusive
Each observation should belong to one category or one cell.
If categories are healthy, infected, and dead, one plant should not be counted in more than one category at the same time.
If observations can belong to multiple categories, the counts are not simple independent category counts.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Assumption 3: observations are independent
One observation should not determine or strongly influence another observation.
Possible violations:

many leaves sampled from the same plant
many people sampled from the same household
repeated observations from the same site
clustered spatial observations
paired before/after measurements

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
When independence fails
If observations are clustered, paired, repeated, or spatially correlated, consider methods that represent the design.
Examples:

logistic regression
multinomial models
mixed-effects models
generalized linear mixed models
permutation tests that respect the sampling structure

The right method depends on how the data were generated.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
section: Assumption 4: expected counts are large enough
text:
Assumption 4: expected counts are large enough
The chi-square test uses an approximation.
The approximation works better when expected counts are not too small.
A common classroom rule is:

Expected counts should generally be at least 5.

The important values are the expected counts, not just observed counts.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Checking expected counts

bird_test$expected |> round(2) |> kable()





Golden Eagle
Red Kite




Glen Affric
23.33
26.67


Glen Nevis
23.33
26.67


Rannoch Moor
23.33
26.67





If expected counts are too small, options include:

collecting more data
combining categories where scientifically sensible
using Fisher’s exact test for small 2 by 2 tables
using simulation-based p-values
using a model designed for sparse counts

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
section: Assumption 5: categories should not be invented after seeing the result
text:
Assumption 5: categories should not be invented after seeing the result
If we repeatedly regroup categories until we find a significant result, the p-value becomes misleading.
Good practice:

define categories before testing where possible
distinguish confirmatory analysis from exploratory analysis
report the analysis process honestly

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
section: Assumption 6: sampling design must support interpretation
text:
Assumption 6: sampling design must support interpretation
The chi-square test can detect a pattern.
It cannot repair a weak study design.
If locations were sampled in different seasons, by different observers, or with different methods, a significant location effect might partly reflect those design differences.
The test detects mismatch.
The study design determines whether the mismatch is interpretable.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
section: What chi-square does not tell you
text:
What chi-square does not tell you
A chi-square test does not automatically tell you practical importance.
With very large samples, tiny deviations can be statistically significant.
With small samples, large-looking deviations may not be statistically significant.
Always inspect observed counts, expected counts, percentages, cell contributions, and scientific context.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Effect size: Cramer’s V
For a contingency table, Cramer’s V is one measure of association strength:
V = sqrt(χ² / [n × min(r − 1, c − 1)])
where:

n is total sample size
r is number of rows
c is number of columns

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Cramer’s V in R

chi <- unname(bird_test$statistic)
n <- sum(birds)
r <- nrow(birds)
c <- ncol(birds)
cramers_v <- sqrt(chi / (n * min(r - 1, c - 1)))
cramers_v

[1] 0.4913538


Cramer’s V is 0 when there is no association.
Larger values indicate stronger association, but interpretation depends on context.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Reporting goodness-of-fit
A concise report should include the test, χ² value, degrees of freedom, p-value, and interpretation.
Example:

A chi-square goodness-of-fit test suggested that the observed die rolls were not consistent with a fair die, χ²(df = 5) = 39.4, p = 1.97^{-7}. Faces 5 and 6 occurred more often than expected under the fair-die model.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Reporting independence
Example:

A chi-square test of independence suggested an association between bird species and location, χ²(df = 2) = 36.21, p = 1.37^{-8}. Inspection of observed and expected counts showed that Golden Eagles were observed more often than expected in Glen Affric and less often than expected in Rannoch Moor, while Red Kites showed the opposite pattern.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Final summary
The chi-square test is used for categorical count data.
Its core idea is:

Compare observed counts with expected counts.

The statistic is:
χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E
Large values mean large discrepancy.
The chi-square distribution tells us whether that discrepancy is unusual under the null hypothesis.

title: Understanding the Chi-Square Test
text:
Final summary: the two tests
Two common introductory chi-square tests are:

Goodness-of-fit
One categorical variable; asks whether observed counts match a proposed distribution.
Independence
Two categorical variables; asks whether the variables are associated.

In both cases, the test is only as meaningful as the null hypothesis, expected counts, assumptions, and study design.

title: Building a Credible Literature Review
text:
This practical guide follows the Week 1 lecture in the same order. Each section turns one lecture concept into a tangible piece of a literature-review workflow. Work with one research topic throughout so that your outputs accumulate into a small, usable review protocol rather than eight disconnected exercises.
